Laurent Sciarra

Laurent Michel Sciarra (born 8 August 1973) is a former French professional basketball player. He one held a Guinness world record for making 60 free throws in 2 minutes. He was inducted into the French Basketball Hall of Fame in 2017

Sciarra began his professional career in 1990, with Hyères-Toulon Var Basket, and he moved to PSG Racing in 1993. He played with PSG until 1997, when he was a member of the club's French League championship season. Sciarra then moved abroad for one season, playing with Ciudad de Huelva in Spain, and Pallacanestro Treviso in Italy, before returning to Paris. In 2001, Sciarra again moved abroad, and spent a season with Panionios in Greece. Following two more seasons with Paris Basket Racing, Sciarra played with the French club BCM Gravelines, for one season. In 2005, he began to play with the French club JDA Dijon, where he stayed until his transfer to French club Entente Orléanaise 45, in 2008.

Sciarra played with France's junior national teams. He played at the 1992 FIBA Europe Under-18 Championship, where he won a gold medal, at the 1993 FIBA Under-21 World Cup, where he won a silver medal, and at the 1994 FIBA Europe Under-20 Championship.

Sciarra was also a member of the senior men's French national team. With France, he played at the 1997 FIBA EuroBasket, the 1999 FIBA EuroBasket, the 2000 Summer Olympic Games, and the 2001 FIBA EuroBasket. He won the silver medal with France at the 2000 Olympics, and he was the best scorer of the 2000 Olympics final, as he scored 19 points against Team USA.

Clean Your Clock

Clean Your Clock is the thirteenth live album by the band Motörhead, released on 10 June 2016, approximately six months after the death of vocalist and bassist Lemmy. Lemmy dedicated the song "Doctor Rock" to Phil Taylor, Motörhead's drummer from 1976-1983 and from 1987-1992, who died a week before the live album was recorded.

The album was recorded during their European 40th Anniversary tour. It is compiled from two sold-out shows at the Zenith in Munich, Germany, on 20 and 21 November 2015 (both nights were filmed but only the first show was released). Unbeknownst to UDR Records at the time, these two shows would turn out to be the last Motörhead live shows that were recorded professionally.

raw:
hiking trail conditions

The mountain park's main ridge trail is opening this weekend after a month of heavy rain, but hikers should still expect a few lingering challenges. Overnight storms left sections of the path slick with mud, and several low-lying areas remain partially submerged. Trail crews have installed temporary boardwalks over the most vulnerable spots, but the boards can be slippery when wet, so sturdy boots with good grip are essential.

Along the lower loop, recent maintenance work has cleared fallen trees and repaired a damaged drainage culvert that was causing water to pool near the creek crossing. The crew also placed new signage to warn about steep drop-offs that have become more pronounced after the erosion. While the trail is officially open, the park service advises that the crossing may be closed after a sudden thunderstorm, so checking the online trail status before heading out is wise.

Wildlife activity has increased as the water levels recede, and hikers are likely to encounter more deer and occasional elk in the early morning. The park's guidelines recommend staying on the marked route to protect both the animals and fragile vegetation that is still recovering from the wet season. Dogs must be leashed, and owners should carry a whistle in case a curious animal approaches.

For those planning a longer trek, the upper ridge sections are still under observation. Recent rock slides have left loose debris on a short stretch near the summit overlook, and the park's rangers have marked the area with orange tape. While the trail is passable, a slow and careful pace is recommended, and any hikers with limited experience should consider turning back before the marked zone.

Overall, the trail is returning to its typical condition, but the lingering effects of the rain mean extra caution is necessary. Pack extra layers, bring waterproof gear, and keep an eye on weather updates throughout the day. With a little preparation, the trail still offers spectacular views and a rewarding hike for anyone willing to respect the temporary challenges.

raw:
ocean tides

The rhythm of the sea is governed by forces far greater than any storm or wind. Tides are the primary manifestation of the gravitational interplay between the Earth, the moon, and the sun. While the moon exerts the strongest pull, creating the familiar cycle of low and high water, the sun contributes a secondary influence that can either amplify or dampen these movements depending on its alignment with our satellite. Understanding this celestial mechanics is crucial for anyone who lives near or depends on the coastline.

For coastal communities, tide predictions are not merely academic curiosities but vital tools for safety. Whether you are a fisherman planning a safe landing, a boater navigating narrow channels, or a casual beachgoer, knowing the exact time and height of the tide can prevent dangerous situations. Low tide exposes hidden rocks and sandbars that become treacherous at high water, while rising tides can quickly flood beach access points that appear dry during the day.

Beyond immediate safety, tides play a critical ecological role. Intertidal zones, which are submerged at high tide and exposed at low tide, host diverse ecosystems. These areas are dynamic habitats where specialized organisms have adapted to withstand drastic changes in water level, temperature, and salinity. The ebb and flow bring nutrient-rich water to these zones, supporting a rich food web that extends from microscopic plankton to large marine mammals.

Climate change is beginning to alter these ancient rhythms. Sea level rise is slowly submerging low-tide areas, changing the duration and depth of exposure for coastal habitats. This shift disrupts local ecology and increases the risk of coastal flooding, particularly when high tides coincide with storm surges. Scientists are closely monitoring these changes to predict how future tide patterns will impact coastal infrastructure and natural reserves.

Respecting the power of the ocean means respecting its moods. Tides are not fixed constants but dynamic forces that respond to astronomical cycles and local geography. By staying informed and vigilant, we can enjoy the beauty of the shore while acknowledging the immense power that shapes it. Whether you are a resident or a visitor, staying attuned to the tides is a fundamental part of living in harmony with the sea.

ocean tides

The rhythm of the sea is governed by forces far greater than any storm or wind. Tides are the primary manifestation of the gravitational interplay between the Earth, the moon, and the sun. While the moon exerts the strongest pull, creating the familiar cycle of low and high water, the sun contributes a secondary influence that can either amplify or dampen these movements depending on its alignment with our satellite. Understanding this celestial mechanics is crucial for anyone who lives near or depends on the coastline.

For coastal communities, tide predictions are not merely academic curiosities but vital tools for safety. Whether you are a fisherman planning a safe landing, a boater navigating narrow channels, or a casual beachgoer, knowing the exact time and height of the tide can prevent dangerous situations. Low tide exposes hidden rocks and sandbars that become treacherous at high water, while rising tides can quickly flood beach access points that appear dry during the day.

Beyond immediate safety, tides play a critical ecological role. Intertidal zones, which are submerged at high tide and exposed at low tide, host diverse ecosystems. These areas are dynamic habitats where specialized organisms have adapted to withstand drastic changes in water level, temperature, and salinity. The ebb and flow bring nutrient-rich water to these zones, supporting a rich food web that extends from microscopic plankton to large marine mammals.

Climate change is beginning to alter these ancient rhythms. Sea level rise is slowly submerging low-tide areas, changing the duration and depth of exposure for coastal habitats. This shift disrupts local ecology and increases the risk of coastal flooding, particularly when high tides coincide with storm surges. Scientists are closely monitoring these changes to predict how future tide patterns will impact coastal infrastructure and natural reserves.

The National Park Service implementation of a new permit system for high-traffic backcountry zones is effective immediately. This measure aims to protect fragile alpine ecosystems and manage crowding at popular campsites. Visitors must understand that carrying a permit is now a strict legal requirement for entering designated trailheads between July and September.

Failure to possess a valid, printed, or digital permit upon inspection by park rangers will result in a significant fine. These penalties are not subject to waiver. The primary goal is conservation, as foot traffic has visibly degraded soil stability and damaged alpine flora in recent seasons. Responsible stewardship requires every hiker to comply with these updated regulations.

Permits can only be reserved through the official online portal. A special waitlist system has been introduced for dates when capacity is fully booked. Users should check their email daily for confirmation messages. Quotas on specific trails like the Glacier Basin loop have been reduced by twenty percent to allow for natural recovery.

Seasonal restrictions include a mandatory quota on group sizes, which are now capped at ten individuals per party. Large groups must split up and secure separate permits. This ensures that trail width usage remains manageable and reduces the impact on wildlife habitats. Single-family trips are encouraged during peak summer weekends to lessen overall congestion.

Customer service hours for the permit desk have been extended to support the increased public demand. Staff are available from six in the morning until ten in the evening via phone support. For immediate assistance with technical issues on the booking site, consult the online help center. We encourage all visitors to plan their itineraries well in advance to ensure a smooth and safe outdoor experience.

Subject: Questions Regarding Home Internet Plans
Dear Ms. Ramirez,
I hope you are doing well. I am reaching out because I am in the process of evaluating home internet options for my family of four, and I would appreciate some clarification on the services your company offers. Over the past year we have experienced occasional slowdowns during evening hours, which has prompted us to look for a more reliable connection that can comfortably support streaming, remote work, and online schooling.
At the moment we are using a basic 50 Mbps plan that was bundled with our cable TV service. While it has generally met our needs, the increasing number of devices in our household-two laptops, three smartphones, a smart TV, and a home office router-means we are often pushing the limits of that bandwidth. We would like to understand what higher-speed tiers are available, especially those that provide a consistent experience for multiple simultaneous video streams and video-conference calls without data throttling.
Could you please outline the different speed tiers you have, along with any data caps or unlimited options? I am particularly interested in plans that start around 150 Mbps and go up to 500 Mbps, as well as any gigabit offerings that might be on the horizon. In addition, it would be helpful to know whether there are any differences in latency or upload speeds between the various packages, since my wife works from home and relies on stable upload performance for large file transfers.
Alongside speed, pricing and contract details are a major factor for us. I would like to know the monthly cost for each tier, whether there are any promotional discounts for new customers, and how long any introductory rates last before standard pricing applies. Information about equipment fees, early-termination penalties, and the possibility of bundling internet with a streaming service or phone line would also be valuable in making a decision.
Finally, could you provide an overview of the installation process? Specifically, I would like to know how long it typically takes to set up a new connection, whether a technician must visit the home, and what kind of modem or router is required. If there are any current promotions for free installation or waived equipment fees, please include those details as well.
Thank you for taking the time to address my questions. I look forward to your response and hope we can find a plan that meets our family's growing needs.
Sincerely,
Jonathan Lee
Homeowner, 742 Maple Street
(555) 219-8743

raw:
home insulation

Imagine opening the curtains on a cold morning and feeling a gentle warmth radiating from your walls rather than a chilling draft. That comfort is not an illusion but the result of superior home insulation acting as a thermal barrier. Most homeowners overlook this aspect until utility bills spike during winter or summer, revealing severe gaps in their building envelope. Proper insulation keeps heat inside during freezing temperatures and blocks out the sweltering heat when the sun is brutal outside, creating a stable indoor climate regardless of the weather.

The materials available for this purpose vary widely, each with distinct properties suited to different structures. Fiberglass batts are a common choice for standard wall cavities due to their low cost and ease of installation. Spray foam offers a seamless seal that expands to fill irregular spaces, significantly improving air tightness. Cellulose, made from recycled paper, provides excellent sound dampening alongside thermal efficiency. Choosing the right material depends heavily on your home's age, layout, and specific problem areas, requiring a careful evaluation before purchase.

Older homes often suffer from degraded insulation that has settled or compressed over decades. This degradation creates drafts and cold spots that make rooms uncomfortable. Checking for these issues can be as simple as feeling for cold drafts near windows or using a thermal imaging camera to visualize heat loss. Identifying these weak points allows for targeted repairs, ensuring that money spent on renovation yields the maximum return in comfort and energy savings for the entire household.

Beyond comfort, proper insulation is a critical investment in energy conservation. A well-insulated home requires less work from its heating and cooling systems, leading to lower monthly utility bills. Over time, these savings can offset the initial installation costs many times over. Furthermore, a tighter building envelope reduces wear and tear on HVAC equipment, extending the life of expensive machines and reducing the frequency of necessary maintenance calls or repairs.

Finally, consider the environmental impact of your home's energy usage. Reducing energy consumption helps lower your carbon footprint, contributing to broader sustainability goals without requiring significant lifestyle changes. By upgrading your insulation, you create a more efficient, resilient home that serves you well for decades. Professional assessment ensures that the installation meets local building codes and optimizes performance for your specific geographic location and climate conditions.

raw:
clinic appointment reminder

Home | About | Contact

A clinic appointment reminder can be the difference between a smooth visit and a missed opportunity for care. Patients often juggle work, family, and transportation, so a timely nudge helps them keep health on the agenda without stress.

Most modern practices use automated systems that send texts or emails 24 to 48 hours before the scheduled time. The message typically includes the date, time, provider name, and any preparation instructions, such as fasting or bringing medication lists. This clarity reduces confusion at check-in.

When a reminder is missed, staff often have to make follow-up calls, which consumes valuable time and can frustrate patients who already feel rushed. Automated reminders free up front-desk employees to focus on more complex tasks, like answering insurance questions or coordinating referrals.

Patients also appreciate the personal touch of a reminder that feels like a friendly check-in rather than a generic alert. Including the clinician's name and a brief, warm greeting can increase the likelihood of attendance and reinforce the patient-provider relationship.

For clinics that serve vulnerable populations, reminders can be tailored to language preferences and accessibility needs. Sending a voice call in the patient's primary language or providing a text with a simple confirmation link ensures that everyone receives the same level of care coordination.

Implementing a reliable reminder system not only boosts appointment adherence but also improves overall clinic efficiency and patient satisfaction.

raw:
home internet plans

Finding the right home internet plan has become as essential as picking a reliable electricity provider. With more families working remotely, streaming in 4K, and gaming online, the bandwidth you choose can affect everything from video calls to late-night movie marathons.

Cable and fiber dominate suburban neighborhoods, offering speeds from 100 Mbps to a gigabit per second. DSL still serves many rural homes, but its 25 Mbps ceiling can feel sluggish for multiple devices. Satellite fills the gaps, though latency and data caps remain drawbacks.

Speed tiers are advertised in megabits per second, but actual performance hinges on network congestion and how many users share the line. Unlimited data is now common, yet some low-cost plans still cap usage at 300 GB, triggering fees if you binge-watch all weekend.

Pricing ranges widely; a basic 100 Mbps plan may start near $30 a month, while a gigabit service can exceed $100. Bundling internet with TV or phone often lowers the combined bill, but watch for early-termination fees and promotional rates that expire after a year.

Before you sign up, check the provider's coverage map for your address and ask neighbors about real-world speeds. Compare total costs, including equipment rental and installation, against the advertised speed. A plan that fits your device count and usage will keep you connected without breaking the bank.

raw:
meeting reschedule

When a meeting needs to be moved, the first priority is clear communication. Most professionals receive dozens of calendar invites each week, so a concise, polite notice that explains the change can prevent confusion and keep the momentum of the agenda intact. An email or a message in the organization's scheduling platform should include the new date and time, the reason for the shift, and a brief reminder of the meeting's purpose.

Timing matters as much as tone. Sending the reschedule notice at least 24 hours in advance gives participants enough room to adjust their own calendars, while a last-minute change should be accompanied by an apology and an offer to accommodate any resulting conflicts. If the meeting involves external partners, consider their time zones and typical working hours to avoid unnecessary inconvenience. A quick phone call or instant message can also help convey urgency when the situation calls for it.

Choosing the right tool can streamline the process. Modern calendar applications allow you to propose new times directly within the invitation, letting attendees vote on alternatives without endless email threads. Some platforms automatically update the meeting link, ensuring that the correct virtual room is used. When using a shared document for the agenda, make sure the revised schedule is reflected there as well, so that everyone can see the most up-to-date information at a glance.

The content of the meeting should be revisited when a reschedule occurs. If the new time falls later in the day, participants may be more fatigued, which could affect the depth of discussion. Adjusting the agenda to prioritize the most critical items early can help maintain focus. In some cases, a shorter, more focused session may be more effective than trying to fit the original plan into a tighter timeframe.

Finally, follow up after the meeting to confirm that the new schedule worked for everyone. A brief thank-you note that acknowledges the flexibility of the attendees reinforces a culture of respect and reliability. Over time, consistently handling reschedules with professionalism builds trust and reduces the friction that can otherwise derail collaborative projects.

raw:
Juan José de Estrada

Juan José de Estrada was a military leader who served as the governor of East Florida from 1811-1812 and again from 1815-1816. Both of his terms were overwhelmed with tension from the Patriot War between the United States and Spain. In 1816 de Estrada was promoted and left Florida for Havana, Cuba.

Juan José de Estrada's father, Pedro de Estrada, was one of the senior military leaders defending Havana from British attack and occupation in 1762. Juan José and his brother Ignacio both joined the military like his father and grandfather before him.

Both of de Estrada's governmental terms were short-lived. His first term as governor was an interim term due to the illness of the former governor, Enrique White. Not all leading Spaniards in Florida welcomed de Estrada's governorship. Manuel López, chief treasury official, did not want a strictly military man in charge of the royal treasury, but he was outvoted. In June of 1811, Estrada received news that Governor White had died and his command was secured. De Estrada's first term started poorly, however, when a massive hurricane hit Florida on October 5, 1811. In response to the hurricane, de Estrada called upon four pre-selected comisarios del barrio, who implemented post-hurricane procedures, visited each house in their neighborhood, and evaluated losses. The four men, José Sánchez, Juan González Montes de Oca, Joaquín Sánchez, and Gaspar Papy, had been chosen for their standing in the community. In his first term, de Estrada also faced a lack of funds to support his troops, undermanned forces, and a threat from the Georgia border. General George Mathews of Georgia attempted to befriend Seminoles in the interior of East Florida, so de Estrada made the decision to spend what little money he had on gifts to Seminole chiefs. His second term was also an interim term. In June of 1815, outgoing governor Don Sebastian Kindelan y O'Regan, knight of the order of Santiago and brigadier of the royal armies, alongside Don Manuel de Castilla, captain of the third battalion of the infantry regiment of Cuba which garrisoned St. Augustine, Florida, swore Juan José de Estrada back into office. On June 28, 1815, de Estrada wrote to Spanish diplomat and Spanish envoy to the United States Luis de Onís that he had taken command of Florida and that Sebastian Kindelan had returned to Cuba. Throughout de Estrada's tenure, skirmishes across the Florida-Georgia border resulted in what became known as the Patriot War. De Estrada communicated with the Governor of Georgia regarding hostilities venturing south of the border. In 1812 he deployed an armed schooner to keep Americans from invading St. Augustine. In 1816 Juan José de Estrada was promoted to colonel and named sergeant-major of the Plaza and Mayor of Havana. José Coppinger was placed in command of East Florida.

.

raw:
neighbourhood safety

Living in a secure neighborhood is more than just a wish; it is a tangible outcome of collective effort and consistent awareness. Safety is not a static condition that exists on its own. It requires active participation from every resident, from the young to the elderly. When neighbors take an interest in their shared environment, the dynamic of the street changes. It shifts from a collection of isolated households into a cohesive community where everyone feels a sense of responsibility for the well-being of the whole. This social fabric acts as a primary deterrent against crime and negligence, creating a buffer that police patrols alone cannot achieve.

Visibility is a powerful tool in maintaining neighborhood security. Crime often thrives in shadows and isolated areas where individuals feel anonymous. Ensuring that walkways, front yards, and common park areas are well-lit can significantly reduce the opportunity for illicit activities. Simple actions, such as leaving a porch light on during dark hours or trimming overgrown bushes that hide entry points, contribute to this sense of openness. Residents should also be mindful of their own visibility. Walking in pairs or groups, especially after sunset, signals to potential wrongdoers that the area is monitored by attentive and connected individuals rather than isolated targets.

Communication lines between residents are just as critical as physical barriers. Knowing who lives next door is the first step toward true safety. Organizing regular neighborhood walks or weekend barbecues helps break down the barriers of urban anonymity. If you do not know your neighbor's name, you are unlikely to notice when something seems off. Establishing a group chat or a simple reporting system allows residents to share observations quickly. A report about a suspicious vehicle or a broken chain link fence becomes a community concern rather than an individual burden. This shared vigilance ensures that small issues are addressed before they escalate into larger problems.

Resilience also depends on preparedness. Every household should have a basic plan for emergencies, whether it is a fire, a power outage, or a medical crisis. Knowing the location of fire exits, having a first aid kit, and understanding how to contact local authorities efficiently can save precious minutes in a crisis. Regularly checking that smoke detectors are functioning and that alarm systems are active is a mundane but vital part of safety. These measures provide a psychological sense of control. When residents feel prepared, they are less likely to panic during unexpected events, allowing them to respond with clarity and calmness.

Ultimately, neighborhood safety is an ongoing process, not a destination. It demands consistency and adaptation. As new families move in or old landmarks disappear, the community must evolve to maintain its protective standards. Trust is the currency of this system. It is built through small, genuine interactions and reinforced by the reliable presence of caring neighbors. When every person on the street feels valued and watched over, the neighborhood becomes a sanctuary. This environment fosters not just safety, but a deep sense of belonging that enriches the daily lives of all who call it home.

raw:
Dexter cattle

The Dexter is an Irish breed of small cattle. It originated in the eighteenth century in County Kerry, in south-western Ireland, and appears to be named after a man named Dexter, who was factor of the estates of Lord Hawarden on Valentia Island. Until the second half of the nineteenth century it was considered a type within the Kerry breed.

The Dexter originated in the eighteenth century in County Kerry, in south-western Ireland, and was apparently named after a man named Dexter, who was factor of the estates of Lord Hawarden on Valentia Island. Rotund short-legged Kerry cattle are documented from the late eighteenth century; the Scottish agriculturalist David Low, writing in 1842, describes them as the "Dexter Breed", and writes "When any individual of a Kerry drove appears remarkably round and short legged, it is common for the country people to call it a Dexter". Until the second half of the nineteenth century the Dexter was considered a type within the Kerry breed; from 1863 it was shown in a separate class at the agricultural shows of the Royal Dublin Society. A joint herd-book, The Kerry and Dexter Herd Book, was established in 1890, and a breed society, the Kerry and Dexter Cattle Society of Ireland, was started in 1917; the name was shortened to the Kerry Cattle Society of Ireland in 1919. It was brought to England in 1882. The breed virtually disappeared in Ireland, but was still maintained as a pure breed in a number of small herds in England and the United States. In 2023 it was reported to DAD-IS by sixteen countries in Africa, the Americas, Europe and Oceania; the largest populations were in Denmark and the United Kingdom. Its conservation status worldwide is listed as 'not at risk', while for Ireland it is listed as 'at risk/critical'.

The cattle are small; heights at the withers for bulls are usually in the range 102-112 cm, for cows about 5 cm less; the average weight of a cow is approximately 325 kg. The coat is usually solid black, but may also be red or dun. The cattle were formerly always horned; in the twenty-first century some polled examples are seen, but the mechanism of introduction of this characteristic has not been identified. Some Dexter cattle carry a gene for chondrodysplasia (a semilethal gene), which is a form of dwarfism that results in shorter legs than unaffected cattle. Chondrodysplasia-affected Dexters are typically 6-8 in shorter in height than unaffected ones. Breeding two chondrodysplasia-affected Dexters together results in a 25% chance that the foetus can abort prematurely. A DNA test is available to test for the chondrodysplasia gene, using tail hairs from the animal. The aborted foetus is commonly called a bulldog, a stillborn calf that has a bulging head, compressed nose, protruding lower jaw, and swollen tongue, as well as extremely short limbs. The occurrence of bulldog foetuses is higher in calves born with a black coat than a red coat, because black coat colour is more common. Short-legged Dexter cattle are considered to be heterozygous, while bulldog foetuses are homozygous for chondrodysplasia genes. Dexters can also be affected with pulmonary hypoplasia with anasarca (PHA), which is an incomplete formation of the lungs with accumulation of a serum fluid in various parts of the tissue of the foetus. Unlike chondrodysplasia, which has many physical signs, PHA shows no outward signs and is only detectable through DNA testing. As with Chondrodysplasia, PHA-affected Dexters should not be bred together. Dexter cattle have short legs compared to other breeds; increased shortness is displayed from the knee to the fetlock. The cattle industry highly values Dexter cattle as they are considered to be hardy, efficient grazers that are able to thrive on poor land.

The Dexter is dual-purpose breed, reared for both milk and beef. Milk yields average about 2250 kg per lactation, although some farms may reach an average of 3000 kg. In flavour and texture the meat is often less good than that of other breeds, especially if it is from a very short-legged animal.

A joint herd-book, The Kerry and Dexter Herd Book, was established in 1890, and a breed society, the Kerry and Dexter Cattle Society of Ireland, was started in 1917; the name was shortened to the Kerry Cattle Society of Ireland in 1919. It was brought to England in 1882. The breed virtually disappeared in Ireland, but was still maintained as a pure breed in a number of small herds in England and the United States. In 2023 it was reported to DAD-IS by sixteen countries in Africa, the Americas, Europe and Oceania; the largest populations were in Denmark and the United Kingdom. Its conservation status worldwide is listed as 'not at risk', while for Ireland it is listed as 'at risk/critical'.

The cattle are small; heights at the withers for bulls are usually in the range 102-112 cm, for cows about 5 cm less; the average weight of a cow is approximately 325 kg. The coat is usually solid black, but may also be red or dun. The cattle were formerly always horned; in the twenty-first century some polled examples are seen, but the mechanism of introduction of this characteristic has not been identified. Some Dexter cattle carry a gene for chondrodysplasia (a semilethal gene), which is a form of dwarfism that results in shorter legs than unaffected cattle. Chondrodysplasia-affected Dexters are typically 6-8 in shorter in height than unaffected ones. Breeding two chondrodysplasia-affected Dexters together results in a 25% chance that the foetus can abort prematurely. A DNA test is available to test for the chondrodysplasia gene, using tail hairs from the animal. The aborted foetus is commonly called a bulldog, a stillborn calf that has a bulging head, compressed nose, protruding lower jaw, and swollen tongue, as well as extremely short limbs. The occurrence of bulldog foetuses is higher in calves born with a black coat than a red coat, because black coat colour is more common. Short-legged Dexter cattle are considered to be heterozygous, while bulldog foetuses are homozygous for chondrodysplasia genes. Dexters can also be affected with pulmonary hypoplasia with anasarca (PHA), which is an incomplete formation of the lungs with accumulation of a serum fluid in various parts of the tissue of the foetus. Unlike chondrodysplasia, which has many physical signs, PHA shows no outward signs and is only detectable through DNA testing. As with Chondrodysplasia, PHA-affected Dexters should not be bred together. Dexter cattle have short legs compared to other breeds; increased shortness is displayed from the knee to the fetlock. The cattle industry highly values Dexter cattle as they are considered to be hardy, efficient grazers that are able to thrive on poor land.

The Dexter is dual-purpose breed, reared for both milk and beef. Milk yields average about 2250 kg per lactation, although some farms may reach an average of 3000 kg. In flavour and texture the meat is often less good than that of other breeds, especially if it is from a very short-legged animal.

Hi Sarah,
I hope your weekend went well. I wanted to reach out regarding our scheduled decision on adopting Max from the county shelter. We came home yesterday and have been spending quality time with him in the living room to see how he handles our daily routine.
Honestly, he is a sweet and gentle soul. He has settled into his new crate nicely and showed very little anxiety when I left on my morning walk. The biggest hurdle has been getting him comfortable with our resident cat, Bella. At first, there were some tense moments, but by late afternoon, they were happily sharing the same carpet square.
I know you said we needed to wait until the full two-week trial period ended before making any final calls. I completely respect that advice and do not want to rush the process. We want to ensure this is the right fit for our family long-term, not just an impulsive decision based on his initial charm.
Could you let me know if we should plan to bring him back on Friday as originally discussed? Also, I am still a bit unsure about the microchip registration fees mentioned in the contract. Do we handle that directly at the shelter, or is there a separate form we need to fill out at home before the finalization date?
Please let me know if there is any other paperwork you need from our side. I am keen to get this sorted so we can focus entirely on adjusting to our new buddy. Thank you for all your guidance so far. It has made the transition feel much less daunting.
Best regards,
David

Subject: Review of the Newly Curated Modernist Wing
Dear Dr. Evans,
I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to share my thoughts after visiting the newly opened exhibition of modernist art at the city museum last weekend. The curation has been meticulously handled, and the flow from the early impresionist experiments to the sharp geometric lines of mid-century constructivism was both logical and deeply engaging. It has been some time since I have seen such a coherent narrative thread drawn through a collection of this magnitude, and the attention to detail in the layout was truly impressive.
The physical installation deserves particular mention. The lighting design was subtle yet effective, ensuring that the pigments of the lesser-known pieces stood out without causing glare on the glass enclosures. I appreciated how the curators used negative space to allow each work to breathe, preventing the overwhelming density that often plagues large collections. This approach forced a slower, more contemplative pace from the visitors. I found myself lingering in front of several smaller canvas works for ten minutes or more, something that rarely happens in the rush of a typical gallery visit.
One specific installation that caught my eye was the interactive display reconstructing the artist's original studio environment. Seeing the raw materials, the scattered sketches, and the half-finished canvases provided a visceral context for the final polished pieces displayed in the next room. It humanized the abstract forms we usually view from a distance, reminding us of the labor and experimentation behind every sharp angle and bold color block. While the audio guide was informative, I think adding more primary source documents from the artists themselves would have added another layer of authenticity to the experience.
Despite its strengths, I did notice a few minor issues regarding crowd management during peak hours. The central hall between the two main sections became quite congested, leading to annoying bottlenecks that disrupted the viewing flow. Implementing a timed entry system or widening the central aisle might alleviate this congestion. Additionally, some of the informational placards were placed at a height that was uncomfortable for shorter visitors, requiring them to crane their necks to read the contextual history. These are small adjustments, but they would significantly enhance overall visitor comfort.
I am confident that this exhibition will serve as a cornerstone for the museum's current season, attracting scholars and casual art lovers alike. The financial investment in proper conservation displays was clearly worth the cost, as the preservation state of the older textiles was exemplary. I recommend extending the run by a few weeks if possible, as word is spreading quickly in local academic circles. I would be happy to discuss these observations in more detail at our next committee meeting. Let me know if you require any further feedback on specific sections.
Best regards,
Sarah Jenkinson
Curatorial Associate

mountain weather

Mountain weather is notoriously fickle, shifting from bright sunshine to sudden snowstorms within minutes. The key to navigating this variability is understanding the forces at work high above the tree line. As air rises along a slope, it expands and cools, often reaching its dew point and forming clouds or precipitation. This process, known as orographic lift, can create localized storms that bear little resemblance to the weather in nearby valleys. Hikers and climbers who respect these micro-climates are more likely to finish their trips safely.

Temperature gradients in the mountains are steeper than on the plains, which means that a 1,000-foot gain in elevation can feel like a 5-degree drop. Even in midsummer, summit temperatures can hover around freezing, while the base enjoys mild, comfortable warmth. Wind also intensifies with altitude, sometimes exceeding 30 miles per hour on exposed ridges. The combination of cold, wind, and low humidity creates a rapid onset of wind-chill, making clothing choices a matter of life and death rather than comfort.

Weather forecasts for mountain regions are improving, but they still lag behind the speed of change on the ground. Radar can miss low-level clouds that cling to peaks, and satellite images may not capture the fine detail of a passing front. The most reliable source of information often comes from on-site observation: cloud base, barometric pressure, and the direction of prevailing winds. Many seasoned hikers carry a compact altimeter and a wind-meter, allowing them to detect subtle shifts that signal an approaching storm.

Safety planning should incorporate the possibility of rapid weather changes. Pack layers that can be added or removed quickly, include a waterproof shell, and keep a headlamp handy even on short day trips. Know your exit routes and set a turnaround time that leaves a comfortable margin before dark. If you notice clouds gathering on the summit while you are still on a lower trail, consider descending early; the mountain will likely retain the moisture and release it as a sudden shower or thunderstorm later in the day.

Finally, respect the mountain's own rhythm. Weather patterns often follow diurnal cycles: clear mornings give way to afternoon clouds, especially on the windward side of a range. By timing your ascent to take advantage of the more stable early hours, you can avoid the most volatile periods. Whether you are a casual weekend hiker or a seasoned alpinist, staying informed, dressing appropriately, and listening to the signs around you will make your experience in the mountains both enjoyable and safe.

I am writing to follow up on our recent discussions regarding the city's long-term strategy for managing the increasing impacts of climate change. As we have seen in the last few summers, the frequency of extreme weather events is not just a statistical projection but a daily reality that affects our infrastructure, public health, and economic stability. The reports from the latest panel highlight that we can no longer rely solely on mitigation strategies to solve this crisis. While reducing emissions remains our global duty, local governments must pivot aggressively toward adaptation measures that ensure our residents remain safe and supported regardless of the warming trajectory we face. I believe this shift requires a fundamental change in how we approach budgeting, urban planning, and emergency services.
Our current infrastructure was designed for a climate that no longer exists. The drainage systems in the eastern district are struggling to handle rainfall levels that used to be once-in-fifty-years events but are now occurring multiple times a decade. This puts our aging sewer systems under immense strain, leading to dangerous backups into residential areas and waterways. We need to prioritize flood resiliency upgrades immediately. This includes investing in green infrastructure such as retention parks, permeable pavements, and expanded wetland buffers. These solutions not only manage stormwater more effectively but also provide valuable ecosystem services that improve air quality and community well-being, offering a return on investment that pure concrete solutions cannot match.
Beyond physical infrastructure, we must address the social dimensions of climate vulnerability. Heat waves are the deadliest weather-related hazard in our region, yet they are often invisible until the emergency rooms are overwhelmed. We need to expand our network of cooling centers, ensure they are accessible to vulnerable populations, and integrate heat risk into our public health warning systems. This is not just about installing more air conditioning units in municipal buildings but about recognizing that low-income neighborhoods, lack of tree canopy, and heat islands in the urban core disproportionately affect the most marginalized groups. Equitable adaptation is essential to maintain social cohesion and prevent the deepening of existing inequalities during crisis periods.
I propose that we establish a dedicated climate adaptation task force within the next fiscal quarter. This group should include representatives from public works, health, transportation, and community advocacy organizations. Their primary mandate should be to conduct a comprehensive risk assessment of critical assets and to draft a five-year implementation roadmap with clear funding mechanisms. I have attached a preliminary framework for this initiative, which outlines potential federal grant opportunities and private-public partnership models that could supplement our municipal budget. I believe that by collaborating with local businesses and academic institutions, we can leverage resources more efficiently and demonstrate leadership to other municipalities in our region.
Thank you for your continued partnership and commitment to building a resilient city. I understand that this is a complex undertaking with significant financial implications, but the cost of inaction is far higher. I would value the chance to review these proposals in person during our next budget meeting. Please let me know if you have any immediate thoughts on the drainage priorities or if you would like me to coordinate with the engineering department to provide more detailed technical assessments before we proceed further. I remain optimistic that with focused effort and strategic planning, we can build a community that is not only safe but thriving in the coming decades.
Best regards,
Elara Vance
Director of Urban Resilience
Office of Civic Affairs

Nest (2025 film)

Nest is a 2025 Swiss short drama film, co-written and directed by Stefania Burla. Starring Anouk Petri, the film follows fifteen-year-old Selma, who feels crushed by her mother's expectations, by those of the Catholic village in the Swiss mountains where she lives, and ultimately by her own. The film had its world premiere in the Concorso Nazionale of the Pardi di Domani competition of the 78th Locarno Film Festival on 15 August 2025, where it was nominated for the Pardino d'Oro SRG SSR for the Best Swiss Short Film.

Anouk Petri as Selma Sarah Juliana Bahmou as Luisa Aira Venzi as Michelle Keira Jöhr as Olivia Ruben Otth as Tobias Nicolas De Peri as Ramon Barbara Terpoorten as Marianne

Nest had its World Premiere at the Concorso Nazionale portion of the Pardi di Domani competition of the 78th Locarno Film Festival on 15 August 2025, and competed for the Pardino d'Oro SRG SSR for the Best Swiss Short Film. It was screened on 9 November 2025 at the 22nd Seville European Film Festival, and then on 13 November 2025, it was screened in the Festivals in the Spotlight Film program at the Zagreb Film Festival.

Trịnh Khả

Trịnh Khả (chữ Hán: 鄭可, 1402 - 1451) close advisor to emperor Lê Thái Tổ, chief ruler of Vietnam during the 1440s, and founder of the powerful Trịnh family.

Trịnh Khả, like most of Lê Lợi's chief aides and generals, was from Thanh Hóa Province which is where Lê Lợi was born. During the decade-long Lam Sơn uprising against the Ming dynasty, Trịnh Khả served as an advisor to Lê Lợi. With victory, Trịnh Khả was elevated to a high position in the new court of Emperor Lê Lợi. Trịnh Khả (and the other councilors) were given the privilege of wearing red silk and were called Hành-khiển. Other members of this new elite were: Nguyễn Trãi, Tran Nguyen Han, Lê Sát, Phạm Văn Xảo, Dinh Liêt, and Lê Ngan. When Lê Lợi died in 1433, Lê Sát was appointed regent for the young emperor, Lê Lợi's second son, Lê Thái Tông. Lê Sát made use of his new power to remove rivals from the government, some were killed (like Phạm Văn Xảo), while others, like Trịnh Khả, were sent away to govern distant provinces of Vietnam. Lê Thái Tông officially came of age in 1438 but found Lê Sát was unwilling to give up his power as regent. Lê Thái Tông looked for political allies and found Trịnh Khả. The new emperor appointed Trịnh Khả to command the Palace Guard. A few months later, Lê Sát was accused of ruling in place of the emperor and with the aid of Khả's guards, Lê Sát was arrested and then condemned to death. Not long after this, Lê Ngan was also removed from power, leaving Trịnh Khả as the main power behind Lê Thái Tông. Officially, Trịnh Khả was the head of the Administrative Bureau (Chinh-su-vien) but the next four years were filled with intrigue as the various noble families in the court plotted to expand their power at the expense of their rivals. Trịnh Khả came out on top of this fight, being promoted to the position of Imperial Councilor shortly before Lê Thái Tông became sick and died in 1442. With the death of the young emperor, the new heir to the throne was an infant Lê Nhân Tông. The government was nominally controlled by the boy's mother, Nguyễn Thị Anh (as Dowager Queen and Regent), but she was very young herself. Real power seems to have been wielded by Trịnh Khả along with Nguyễn Xí, Le Thu and two generals: Dinh Liêt and Pham Boi. The government of the oligarchy was not very active but they sent six missions to the Ming Court. Some of the missions were complaints about raids by the Champa kingdom into Vietnam. In 1446, the government launched an attack on the Champa. The campaign was reasonably successful as the Vietnamese army captured the capital city of Vijaya but they lost the city to a counter-attack a year later. This was the forerunner of the 1470 campaign which would destroy the Champa. As the years passed, Queen Nguyễn Thị Anh came into greater conflict with the Trịnh Khả and the other oligarchs who ruled the country. The Queen gained some support from the Confucian scholars who had passed the Imperial examinations and tried to rule much like their Chinese colleges to the north ruled in the Ming imperial system. The nobles in turn tried to limit the power of the scholars and maintain their own control over the government. For reasons lost to history, the Queen ordered Trịnh Khả and his eldest son executed in August 1451. Two years later, upon the official enthronement of Lê Nhân Tông (at the age of 12), Trịnh Khả was pardoned and new lands were given to the Trịnh family. The Trịnh family continued to be a major noble family in Việt Nam. In 1545, a great-grandson named Trịnh Kiểm, took control of a large part of Vietnam. His descendants ruled the north for the next 240 years (see the Trịnh Lords for details). Three hundred years later, the Vietnamese officer, Lê Quý Đôn, said of Trịnh Khả he "served the public good, exhausted his virtue (on it), and considered the correction of evil and the presentation of instruction to be his own duty".

This history is based on the doctoral thesis of John K. Whitmore "The Development of the Le Government in Fifteenth Century Vietnam" (Cornell University, 1968). The thesis is mostly concerned with the structure and make-up of the Le government from 1427 to 1471.

Trịnh Khả, like most of Lê Lợi's chief aides and generals, was from Thanh Hóa Province which is where Lê Lợi was born. During the decade-long Lam Sơn uprising against the Ming dynasty, Trịnh Khả served as an advisor to Lê Lợi. With victory, Trịnh Khả was elevated to a high position in the new court of Emperor Lê Lợi. Trịnh Khả (and the other councilors) were given the privilege of wearing red silk and were called Hành-khiển. Other members of this new elite were: Nguyễn Trãi, Tran Nguyen Han, Lê Sát, Phạm Văn Xảo, Dinh Liêt, and Lê Ngan. When Lê Lợi died in 1433, Lê Sát was appointed regent for the young emperor, Lê Lợi's second son, Lê Thái Tông. Lê Sát made use of his new power to remove rivals from the government, some were killed (like Phạm Văn Xảo), while others, like Trịnh Khả, were sent away to govern distant provinces of Vietnam. Lê Thái Tông officially came of age in 1438 but found Lê Sát was unwilling to give up his power as regent. Lê Thái Tông looked for political allies and found Trịnh Khả. The new emperor appointed Trịnh Khả to command the Palace Guard. A few months later, Lê Sát was accused of ruling in place of the emperor and with the aid of Khả's guards, Lê Sát was arrested and then condemned to death. Not long after this, Lê Ngan was also removed from power, leaving Trịnh Khả as the main power behind Lê Thái Tông. Officially, Trịnh Khả was the head of the Administrative Bureau (Chinh-su-vien) but the next four years were filled with intrigue as the various noble families in the court plotted to expand their power at the expense of their rivals. Trịnh Khả came out on top of this fight, being promoted to the position of Imperial Councilor shortly before Lê Thái Tông became sick and died in 1442. With the death of the young emperor, the new heir to the throne was an infant Lê Nhân Tông. The government was nominally controlled by the boy's mother, Nguyễn Thị Anh (as Dowager Queen and Regent), but she was very young herself. Real power seems to have been wielded by Trịnh Khả along with Nguyễn Xí, Le Thu and two generals: Dinh Liêt and Pham Boi. The government of the oligarchy was not very active but they sent six missions to the Ming Court. Some of the missions were complaints about raids by the Champa kingdom into Vietnam. In 1446, the government launched an attack on the Champa. The campaign was reasonably successful as the Vietnamese army captured the capital city of Vijaya but they lost the city to a counter-attack a year later. This was the forerunner of the 1470 campaign which would destroy the Champa. As the years passed, Queen Nguyễn Thị Anh came into greater conflict with the Trịnh Khả and the other oligarchs who ruled the country. The Queen gained some support from the Confucian scholars who had passed the Imperial examinations and tried to rule much like their Chinese colleges to the north ruled in the Ming imperial system. The nobles in turn tried to limit the power of the scholars and maintain their own control over the government. For reasons lost to history, the Queen ordered Trịnh Khả and his eldest son executed in August 1451. Two years later, upon the official enthronement of Lê Nhân Tông (at the age of 12), Trịnh Khả was pardoned and new lands were given to the Trịnh family. The Trịnh family continued to be a major noble family in Việt Nam. In 1545, a great-grandson named Trịnh Kiểm, took control of a large part of Vietnam. His descendants ruled the north for the next 240 years (see the Trịnh Lords for details). Three hundred years later, the Vietnamese officer, Lê Quý Đôn, said of Trịnh Khả he "served the public good, exhausted his virtue (on it), and considered the correction of evil and the presentation of instruction to be his own duty".
This history is based on the doctoral thesis of John K. Whitmore "The Development of the Le Government in Fifteenth Century Vietnam" (Cornell University, 1968). The thesis is mostly concerned with the structure and make-up of the Le government from 1427 to 1471.

The upcoming special exhibition, "Silent Voices: Textiles of the Early Modern Period," will commence its public run on the first of November. Curatorial staff have finalized the installation layout, ensuring that the flow of visitors allows for comfortable viewing without overcrowding the smaller display cases. This exhibition features forty-six artifacts, primarily shawls, embroidery samplers, and household linens, sourced from both the museum's permanent collection and long-term loans from three private estates. The theme focuses on the intersection of domestic labor and regional trade networks, offering visitors a tangible connection to the daily lives of women in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. We are particularly proud of the newly acquired chintz patterns, which illustrate the complex shipping routes between Europe and the Indian subcontinent.

Environmental controls within the Gallery North wing have been adjusted to meet the specific needs of the organic materials on display. Light levels will be capped at thirty lux to prevent accelerated fading of the dyes, which remain sensitive despite decades of stable storage. Humidity levels will be maintained at a relative humidity of fifty percent, with a permissible variance of no more than three percent. Conservators have noted that the linen items require slightly tighter tolerance than the cotton pieces, which is why two additional hygrometers have been installed near the primary display case. These precautions are essential to ensure the longevity of the artifacts while preserving the visual integrity of the展览 for the duration of the six-month run.

Security protocols have been updated to reflect the high value of several loaned pieces. All glass panels have been reinforced with shatter-resistant film, and the central display case houses a motion-sensor alarm that triggers immediate notification to the security control room. Visitors are asked to refrain from placing bags on any surface near the exhibits, and ushers will be stationed at the main entrance and midway through the gallery to provide assistance and enforce these guidelines. Additionally, strict no-flash photography policies apply throughout the space to protect the delicate fibers from UV exposure. Staff have been briefed on how to politely remind guests of these rules without disrupting the immersive atmosphere of the exhibition.

Educational programming aligned with the exhibition content begins in the week before opening. School groups will access a dedicated workshop area where they can engage with reproductions of the textiles, allowing them to understand weaving techniques without risking damage to the originals. Docents have completed thorough training on the historical context of each piece, including the social implications of sumptuary laws that dictated who could wear certain fabrics. Interpreted tours will be available in both English and the museum's secondary language of outreach to broaden accessibility. Feedback from the pilot tours suggests strong interest in the stories behind the maker's marks, which we will highlight with larger, more legible didactic panels in the final layout.

The exhibition catalogue, featuring essays from four leading historians in textile studies, is now available for purchase at the museum shop and online. Proceeds from catalogue sales directly support the conservation fund, ensuring future costs for repair and storage are covered. We anticipate high attendance during the final weekend before the holidays, and consequently, timed entry tickets will be mandatory for general admissions to manage crowd density. The public is encouraged to visit during weekday afternoons for a more relaxed experience. As the opening approaches, the team is focused on final quality checks, including verifying all label information and ensuring the lighting cues transition smoothly between the introductory and main gallery spaces.

conference registration

The moment the call for papers closes, the real work begins for conference organizers. The transition from academic curation to operational logistics is where many events stall. Registration systems serve as the primary interface between the organizers and the attendees, handling the complex flow of financial transactions, permission checks, and data collection. A robust setup requires more than just a payment gateway; it demands a seamless user experience that can withstand the pressure of thousands of simultaneous sign-ups. If the platform feels sluggish or confusing, potential participants often abandon their carts, leading to significant revenue loss and a shrunken audience base. Therefore, selecting the right software is the first critical step in this phase of the project.

Pricing strategies add another layer of complexity to the registration process. Most conferences utilize a tiered structure with early-bird discounts to encourage early commitment and smooth out cash flow. There are also often different rates for students, professionals, and industry sponsors, each requiring specific validation methods. Organizers must ensure that these tiers are clearly defined and easily accessible. Ambiguity in pricing terms leads to increased support tickets and frustrated users who feel they were misled. The interface should allow users to select their specific category without needing to consult a separate FAQ page. Clarity in this area builds trust and reduces administrative burden during the critical pre-event period.

Data verification is perhaps the least glamorous but most vital aspect of registration management. Conferences require accurate headcounts for catering, badge printing, and capacity planning for sessions. This means the registration portal must integrate seamlessly with attendee databases and potentially with hotel reservation systems. Automated checks can flag duplicate entries or incomplete profiles, prompting immediate follow-up. Manual data entry is a breeding ground for errors, so automated synchronization is essential. When a user updates their dietary restrictions or emergency contact on the portal, that information should instantly reflect in the backend system that generates the final attendee list. This ensures that on-site operations run smoothly and that safety protocols are strictly adhered to without extra manual labor.

Accessibility and inclusivity should not be an afterthought but a core feature of the registration design. Forms must be compatible with screen readers and intuitive for users with varying levels of digital literacy. Long-winded forms with excessive mandatory fields discourage sign-up and risk alienating parts of the academic community. A streamlined process respects the user's time and signals that the organizers value a diverse and accessible participant base. Additionally, clear communication about visa letters or accommodation links directly through the confirmation email can save weeks of back-and-forth correspondence. These small touches significantly enhance the overall perception of the event's professionalism and care for its international community.

In the final days leading up to the event, the registration portal transforms into a hub for last-minute changes and cancellations. The policy on refunds and transfers must be crystal clear to avoid disputes. As the event begins, the system supports check-in processes, providing organizers with real-time data on actual attendance versus expected numbers. This live data is invaluable for making immediate adjustments to room availability and food services. A well-managed registration process ensures that the focus of the conference remains on the content and networking, not on logistical hiccups. The invisible efficiency of the backend allows the event to feel effortless to the attendees, who simply show up and engage with the material around them.

Subject: New After-Hours Hours for Downtown Branch
Dear Patron,
I am writing to inform you of a significant update to our operating schedule. Effective next month, the downtown branch will extend its evening hours. We are now open until 9:00 PM on weekdays. This change is designed to accommodate our community members who work standard office hours and need access to resources after their workday concludes.
We have also launched a new digital initiative. Patrons can now borrow audiobooks and e-magazines with a single tap using our updated mobile app. This service eliminates the need for physical media and allows for instant access to our collection from anywhere. It is free of charge for all active library card holders.
To support local students, we are introducing a dedicated homework help zone. This area will be staffed by volunteer tutors every Tuesday and Thursday from 3:00 PM to 6:00 PM. Parents and guardians are welcome to join and observe the sessions. We believe this initiative will provide a safe and supportive environment for young learners to complete their assignments.
Please note that parking rates at the municipal garage behind the library will increase slightly next quarter. We recommend using the public transit system or car-sharing options to visit the branch. The 12nd Street bus stop is located just out front and runs every fifteen minutes during peak hours.
If you have questions about these changes, please visit the circulation desk or email us directly. We are committed to serving your needs and looking forward to seeing you at the library soon. Your continued support helps us maintain these essential community resources.
Sincerely,
The Public Library Team

Chirnside Parish Church

Chirnside Parish Church is a kirk of the Church of Scotland. It is situated on the B6355 road between Duns and Eyemouth in the old county of Berwickshire, now part of the Scottish Borders, at grid reference NT869560. The town of Chirnside is 6 miles (9.7 km) east of Duns, and 9 miles (14 km) north-west of Berwick-upon-Tweed. Jim Clark (Racing Driver) is also buried here.

The first records of Chirnside and its church came in the early 12th century during the reign of King Edgar of Scotland (1097-1107), in a charter granting the lands and church to the monks of Durham. The 12th-century church was known as Ecclesia de Chirnyside and it was valued at 50 merks. The first church at Chirnside was a plain rectangular building with a thatched roof and earthen floor. The altar dominated the east end and a priest would conduct daily mass, probably from a pulpit near the altar. The Ecclesia de Chirnyside was dedicated, like many other church establishments in the area, by David de Bernham, Bishop of St Andrews, on 13 April 1242. In 1524 a young man named Luke Acheson, who lived in the village, was keeping watch from the tower of the church, and was killed by six English freebooters.

It would appear the old church was badly damaged at the Reformation as the body of the church was extensively repaired in 1573, and the first minister of the new reformed faith was not installed until that year (see list of early ministers). In 1581, during the reign of King James VI of Scotland, the church was mentioned in a national list of Presbyteries. There was further extensive renewal in 1757, and a new manse was built for the minister. A wall on the western tower was retained in the renovations, with an engraved plate declaring "Helpe the pyr" (Help the poor) and the date 1573. A Norman archway was retained from the 12th-century church.

In 1904, following the death of Lady Tweedmouth and her burial at the west end of the church, her husband, Edward Marjoribanks, 2nd Baron Tweedmouth completely reshaped the interior of the church. He built a hall, a new vestry and added a new tower. Following the Baron's death, his son erected a memorial gateway in memory of his father. The already united churches of Free Church and United Free Church, joined the Church of Scotland kirk in 1929. The North Church closed in 1973 but reopened in 1984 as a community centre. The United Presbyterian Church of Scotland building was demolished in 1982. Chirnside Parish Church is a category B listed building. World Champion Formula One driver Jim Clark (1936-1968) was buried in Chirnside Kirkyard, after his death in April 1968 at the Hockenheimring in Germany.

raw:
local bus timetables

Missing the early morning commuter bus can turn a planned workday into a chaotic scramble for alternative transport. For residents of suburban districts, understanding the precise timings is not just a matter of convenience but a necessity for maintaining professional commitments. The current schedule updates often go unnoticed by regular riders who rely on outdated paper copies, leading to frustrating waits at crowded shelters during rush hour.

The transit authority recently released the revised winter timetables, which shift several peak service intervals by five to ten minutes. These changes are designed to accommodate increased heating reliability across the vehicle fleet and to optimize turnaround times at major hubs. Riders should note that the line 42 express now departs the central station at 07:15 instead of 07:05, providing a slightly longer buffer for boarding but requiring a slightly earlier departure from home.

Home | About | Contact

Digital access has become the standard for verifying real-time adjustments. The official mobile application now features predictive arrival alerts based on GPS tracking, which is particularly useful during inclement weather when delays are common. Users report that relying solely on physical shelter boards is no longer sufficient, as maintenance outages can render information stale by several minutes, making the app the most reliable source for accuracy.

For those without smartphones, regional news outlets and community newsletters provide weekly summaries of significant schedule changes. Local librarians also offer printed cheat sheets upon request, highlighting key morning and afternoon stops. It is advisable to cross-reference these physical guides with the online portal before making long-term travel plans, as temporary diversions due to roadworks are not always reflected in static documents.

Planning ahead remains the best strategy to avoid stress during your daily commute. Arriving at the stop ten minutes early provides a safety net against minor operational hiccups. By staying informed through multiple channels, commuters can navigate their routine with greater confidence, ensuring they reach their destinations on time despite the inevitable fluctuations inherent in public transport systems.

raw:
product launch plan

A successful product launch begins long before the release date, with a clear roadmap that aligns every department around a single vision. Marketing, product development, sales, and customer support must collaborate from day one, defining the target audience, key messaging, and measurable goals. By mapping out milestones such as prototype testing, beta feedback, and press outreach, the team can anticipate roadblocks and allocate resources efficiently.

The first phase focuses on market validation. Conducting surveys, focus groups, and competitor analysis provides insight into the real problems the product solves and the price point customers are willing to pay. These findings shape the positioning statement and help craft a compelling story that resonates with early adopters. A well-documented value proposition becomes the cornerstone of all subsequent communications.

Next comes the pre-launch buzz. Teaser campaigns on social media, influencer partnerships, and a carefully timed email drip sequence build anticipation without revealing too much detail. Offering exclusive previews or limited-time pre-order incentives can convert curiosity into commitment. Meanwhile, the sales team prepares demo kits, training materials, and objection-handling scripts to ensure every sales conversation feels polished and confident.

On launch day, execution must be flawless. A coordinated press release, live event webcast, and real-time social media monitoring create a synchronized splash across channels. Customer support lines are staffed with product experts ready to address the surge of inquiries, while analytics dashboards track downloads, sign-ups, and sentiment in real time. Rapid response to any technical hiccup or negative feedback preserves credibility and momentum.

Finally, post-launch analysis closes the loop. Teams review performance against the original KPIs, gather user feedback, and identify feature requests for future iterations. A debrief meeting highlights what worked, what didn't, and how processes can be refined for the next rollout. By treating the launch as a continuous learning cycle, companies turn a single product debut into a catalyst for long-term growth.

To all Department Heads and Field Operations Managers,

This memorandum outlines the updated protocols for integrating climate adaptation strategies into our regional infrastructure maintenance cycles. Recent meteorological data confirms that the projection periods for severe weather events are shifting earlier in the year, necessitating a proactive rather than reactive approach to asset protection. The goal is no longer merely to withstand storm damage but to enhance the resilience of our water, power, and transit networks against prolonged periods of heat, drought, and intensified precipitation. Consequently, all capital improvement plans submitted for the upcoming fiscal year must include a dedicated section on adaptive capacity assessments to ensure long-term viability.

The first priority area involves the reinforcement of drainage systems in low-lying urban zones. Historical flood models have proven insufficient for the volume and velocity of rainfall we are currently observing. Engineering teams are directed to review aging outfall culverts and expand channel capacities where hydraulic modeling indicates a risk of exceeding design thresholds. This is not simply a matter of replacing concrete; it requires a comprehensive review of surface permeability throughout the district. We must prioritize the installation of green infrastructure solutions, such as bioswales and permeable paving, in areas with high impervious coverage to naturally infiltrate stormwater before it reaches overwhelmed municipal pipes.

In parallel, the energy sector division must accelerate the transition to distributed and decentralized power resources. Centralized grids remain vulnerable to cascading failures during extreme heat waves or ice storms. Therefore, the retrofitting of substations with climate-resilient hardware is now a mandatory component of routine upgrades, not an optional enhancement. Workers should begin mapping critical load centers that serve hospitals and emergency services to identify where microgrid connectivity can be established. These localized networks must be capable of islanding operations, ensuring that essential services continue even if the main transmission lines are compromised by falling debris or downed towers.

HR and workforce development offices must also align their training curricula with these operational shifts. Maintenance crews need specialized certifications in hydraulic modeling and rapid-response emergency engineering. It is no longer sufficient to train technicians only on standard repair procedures; they must understand the environmental stressors that cause failures. We are allocating funds for cross-disciplinary workshops where civil engineers and field operators collaborate on mock scenarios involving compound events, such as simultaneous flooding and power outages. This fosters a shared understanding of system interdependencies and improves decision-making speed during actual crises.

Finally, please note that the Financial Oversight Committee will now tie a portion of annual performance bonuses to the successful implementation of these adaptation metrics. Budget requests that do not justify the necessity of climate-specific upgrades will face stricter scrutiny and likely rejection. We are moving beyond theoretical planning into the phase of tangible execution. Your department heads are expected to submit revised implementation timelines within thirty days, detailing specific milestones and resource allocations. This is a sustained effort that requires consistent attention and investment. Let us treat this shift in strategy as a fundamental restructuring of how we view public safety and infrastructure longevity.

To all Valley Estates residents,
The annual municipal water quality report for the southwest district has been finalized and is now available for your review. Our engineering team conducted over four thousand sample tests across the entire grid to ensure compliance with federal and state safety standards. The results indicate that our water remains consistently safe for consumption, with no detected contaminants exceeding the allowed limits.
Key pollutants such as lead, arsenic, and nitrates were monitored closely this year. All samples registered at levels well below the regulatory thresholds, confirming the effectiveness of our current treatment processes. You will notice that the chlorine levels have been slightly reduced compared to last year, resulting in a cleaner taste for many households.
We also performed comprehensive testing for microorganisms and algal toxins. The data shows zero presence of harmful bacteria or viral agents. Furthermore, the pH balance stayed within the optimal range of 6.8 to 7.4, which prevents corrosion in older plumbing systems. This stability is crucial for maintaining the integrity of your home infrastructure over time.
If you have specific health concerns or elderly family members who are sensitive to trace minerals, we encourage a review of the full technical appendix. We have included a plain-language summary that breaks down these complex figures into easy-to-understand terms. You can find all documents linked in the center of your community portal dashboard for immediate access.
Please read through the entire report to familiarize yourself with the new filtration schedule. We are committed to maintaining transparency regarding the water that flows through your pipes every day. Your trust is our top priority, and we will continue to refine our methods to deliver the highest quality water possible.
Sincerely,
Elena Rostova
Director of Utilities

Freinet classification

The Freinet classification ("To organise everything") is used in the libraries of some elementary schools, and was invented by Célestin Freinet to facilitate the easy finding of documents, and the use of the "Bibliothèque de Travail". The principles are simple: Everything is split into 12 major divisions. 12 subdivisions along the principles of the Dewey Decimal system are then divided into 10, and then 10 again. Because of its logical classifications based on school work, this classification is seen by some educators to be more natural and more logical to students than official classifications based on organizational criteria. The last revision took place in 1984. It is still used, in addition to keywords, in IT and some data information organization systems.

00 General 01 English Dictionaries 02 Dictionaries in foreign languages 03 Bilingual, trilingual, ... dictionaries 04 Other Dictionaries (proper names, places, ...) 05 Encyclopedias 06 Repertory, bibliographies 07 Reference works (textbooks)

11 Land (geology) 12 Relief 13 Freshwater 14 The oceans and seas 15 The climates and vegetation 16 Heaven (astronomy) 17 Nature and Life (ecology)

30 General study of the body (in humans and animals) 31 The health of humans 32 Mammals (except humans) 33 Birds 34 Reptiles and amphibians 35 Fish 36 Insects (articulated) 37 Other articulated 38 Shellfish 39 Other animals

60 General 61 Sources of energy and engines 62 Mining and quarrying 63 Metals 64 Chemical Industry 65 Textile and clothing industry 66 Building industry, housing and furniture 67 Other Industries

71 The city, the municipality 72 Trade 73 Road Transport 74 Rail transport 75 Inland waterway transport 76 Maritime Transport 77 Air transportation and space 78 Post, Telecommunications and IT 79 Travel and Tourism

G0 The study of geography G1 General Geography G2 Geography locally and regionally G3 Our country G4 Europe G5 Asia G6 Africa G7 America G8 Oceania G9 The Polar World

H1 Prehistory H2 The East, Greece H3 Rome and the early Middle Ages (from -700 to 987) H4 Middle Ages (from 987 to 1492) H5 Absolute monarchy (1492 to 1789) H6 Struggles for Democracy (1789 to 1848) H7 Organization of the Republic (1848 to 1914) H8 Contemporary history (1914-present)
