dormitory rules

Living on campus brings a sense of independence, but it also means sharing space with dozens of other students. The dormitory rules are designed to keep that shared environment safe, comfortable, and conducive to study. Most campuses start the semester with a handbook that outlines everything from quiet hours to kitchen etiquette, and while the specifics can vary, the underlying goals are the same: respect, safety, and community. Understanding these expectations early can prevent misunderstandings and help you settle in more quickly.

One of the most frequently cited rules concerns noise levels. Quiet hours typically begin at 10 p.m. on weekdays and 11 p.m. on weekends, extending until the early morning. During these times, music should be kept at a low volume, and conversations in hallways are expected to be brief and soft. If you have a late-night study session, using headphones is not just courteous-it's often a requirement. Many dorms also limit the use of musical instruments after a certain hour to avoid disrupting neighbors who may be trying to sleep or focus on coursework.

Cleanliness is another cornerstone of dorm life. Residents are expected to keep their personal rooms tidy and to take responsibility for common areas such as lounges, laundry rooms, and bathrooms. Trash should be taken out regularly, and recycling bins must be used correctly. The rules usually prohibit the storage of hazardous materials, such as gasoline or fireworks, and limit the amount of food that can be kept in shared kitchens. By following these guidelines, you help maintain a pleasant environment for everyone and reduce the likelihood of pest infestations or fire hazards.

Safety protocols extend beyond fire prevention. Most dorms require all occupants to have a valid student ID visible at all times, and many enforce a guest registration system. Guests are generally limited to a certain number of nights per week, and they must be escorted by their host while in the building. Alcohol consumption is often restricted to residents of legal drinking age and may be prohibited entirely in some institutions. Violations of these policies can lead to disciplinary action, ranging from warnings to loss of housing privileges.

Respect for personal property is a rule that is sometimes overlooked but is crucial for fostering trust among residents. Borrowing items without permission, taking another student's food from the communal fridge, or tampering with another's lock is considered a serious breach of conduct. Most dorms have a clear process for reporting lost or stolen items, and security cameras are frequently installed in hallways and entrances to deter misconduct. Acting responsibly not only protects you but also reinforces a culture of mutual respect.

Finally, many dormitory agreements include a clause about academic integrity and community involvement. Residents are encouraged to participate in floor meetings, volunteer for resident-assistant training, and attend informational sessions about campus resources. Engaging in these activities helps you build a supportive network and demonstrates a commitment to the dorm's collective well-being. By adhering to the established rules and contributing positively to the community, you create a living environment that supports both personal growth and academic success.

Kalevalsky District

Kalevalsky District (Russian: Ка́левальский райо́н; Karelian: Kalevalan piiri) is an administrative district (raion), one of the fifteen in the Republic of Karelia, Russia. It is located in the northwest of the republic and borders with Finland in the west, Loukhsky District in the north, Kemsky and Muyezersky Districts in the east, and with the territory of the town of republic significance of Kostomuksha in the south. The area of the district is 13,316 square kilometers (5,141 sq mi). Its administrative center is the urban locality (an urban-type settlement) of Kalevala. As of the 2010 Census, the total population of the district was 8,321, with the population of Kalevala accounting for 54.4% of that number.

There are many lakes within the district, and wetlands account for 30% of the district's territory. Natural resources include molybdenum, iron ore, quartzite, copper, and peat.

Within the framework of administrative divisions, Kalevalsky District is one of the fifteen in the Republic of Karelia and has administrative jurisdiction over one urban-type settlement (Kalevala) and eight rural localities. As a municipal division, the district is incorporated as Kalevalsky Municipal District. The urban-type settlement of Kalevala and one rural locality (the settlement of Kuusiniemi) are incorporated into an urban settlement, while the remaining seven rural localities are incorporated into three rural settlements within the municipal district. The urban-type settlement of Kalevala serves as the administrative center of both the administrative and municipal district.

raw:
List of forts in Washington County, Pennsylvania

This article is a list of forts in Washington County, Pennsylvania. During the colonial era and the American Revolution, Washington County, Pennsylvania was on the American Frontier. The forts provided protection for settlers from attacks by Indians who already lived in the area.

Doddridge's Fort was a series of stockaded log cabins in Washington County, Pennsylvania. It was built c. 1773 by John Doddridge as a refuge for settlers in area, which was then the American frontier. The fort was located in present-day Independence Township, Washington County, Pennsylvania. The attack on Doddridge's Fort was recorded in historian's Samuel Kercheval 1883 history A History of the Valley of Virginia. The fort was a frequent stop for Methodist circuit riders, including Francis Asbury. It was also the childhood home of priest-physician Joseph Doddridge, author of the widely cited Notes on the Settlement and Indian Wars of the Western Parts of Virginia and Pennsylvania, and his brother Philip Doddridge, a leading advocate for democratization on behalf of western Virginians. On May 28, 1947, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker at Pa. 844 west of Pa. 231 at Sugar Run Road, 2.5 miles (4.0 km) west of West Middletown, Pennsylvania, noting the importance of Doddridge's Fort to the history of the commonwealth. The actual location of the fort was north of the marker. In 2003, plans were developed for the Washington County Historical Society to create a replica of Doddridge's Fort at Cross Creek County Park. The facility was to have been known as The Washington County Frontier Experience Center.

Lindley's Fort was a blockhouse established by frontier settler Demas Lindley near Ten Mile Creek in what is now the village of Prosperity in Morris Township, Washington County. County historian Alfred Creigh described it as "one of the strongest forts in the western country, because it most exposed to the hostile incursions of the savage inhabitants." Frontier settlers erected additional cabins near the fort as temporary homes during times of increased danger in order to easily retreat with the fort's walls. In 2011, Lindley's Fort became the subject of dispute. Archaeologists and local historians expressed concern that natural gas extraction operator Range Resources planned to construct a drilling pad access road through the historic site.

Miller's Blockhouse was a blockhouse built in about 1780 by Jacob Miller Sr., a pioneer in American Frontier in present-day Washington County, Pennsylvania. The fort served to protect settlers in the Dutch Fork area from Indian attacks. On March 31, 1782, the fort was attacked, and Ann Hupp led a heroic defense. On Wednesday, May 28, 1947, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker on U.S. 40, 3.5 miles (5.6 km) west of Claysville, noting the importance of Miller's Blockhouse to the history of Pennsylvania. The actual site of the blockhouse is 3 miles (4.8 km) north.

Rice's Fort was a fortified blockhouse in present-day Washington County, Pennsylvania. During the American Revolution, it was built by Abraham Rice along Buffalo Creek. In September 1782, the occupants successfully held off a siege by Indians. The attack on Rice's Fort was recorded in historian's Samuel Kercheval 1883 history A History of the Valley of Virginia. In 1973, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker at U.S. 40 at Lake Road, 3.5 miles (5.6 km) west of Claysville, noting the importance of Rice's Fort to the history of Pennsylvania.

Wolff's Fort was a stockaded log house built in about 1780 by Jacob Wolfe. The Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission describes it as "one of the most important forts in the area." On May 28, 1947, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker at U.S. 40, 3.3 miles (5.3 km) southwest of Washington, noting the importance of Wolff's Fort to the history of Pennsylvania.

Doddridge, Joseph; Narcissa Doddridge; John S. Ritenour; William Thomas Lindsey (1912). "The Frontier Forts of Washington County". Notes on the Settlement and Indian Wars of the Western Parts of Virginia and Pennsylvania from 1763 to 1783: Inclusive, Together with a Review of the State of Society and Manners of the First Settlers of the Western Country. The New Werner Company. pp. 310-315. Albert, George Dallas (1916). Report of the Commission to Locate the Site of the Frontier Forts of Pennsylvania: The frontier forts of western Pennsylvania. Vol. 2 (2 ed.). Harrisburg, Pennsylvania: Wm. Stanley Ray, State Printer.

The fort was located in present-day Independence Township, Washington County, Pennsylvania. The attack on Doddridge's Fort was recorded in historian's Samuel Kercheval 1883 history A History of the Valley of Virginia. The fort was a frequent stop for Methodist circuit riders, including Francis Asbury. It was also the childhood home of priest-physician Joseph Doddridge, author of the widely cited Notes on the Settlement and Indian Wars of the Western Parts of Virginia and Pennsylvania, and his brother Philip Doddridge, a leading advocate for democratization on behalf of western Virginians. On May 28, 1947, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker at Pa. 844 west of Pa. 231 at Sugar Run Road, 2.5 miles (4.0 km) west of West Middletown, Pennsylvania, noting the importance of Doddridge's Fort to the history of the commonwealth. The actual location of the fort was north of the marker. In 2003, plans were developed for the Washington County Historical Society to create a replica of Doddridge's Fort at Cross Creek County Park. The facility was to have been known as The Washington County Frontier Experience Center.

Lindley's Fort was a blockhouse established by frontier settler Demas Lindley near Ten Mile Creek in what is now the village of Prosperity in Morris Township, Washington County. County historian Alfred Creigh described it as "one of the strongest forts in the western country, because it most exposed to the hostile incursions of the savage inhabitants." Frontier settlers erected additional cabins near the fort as temporary homes during times of increased danger in order to easily retreat with the fort's walls. In 2011, Lindley's Fort became the subject of dispute. Archaeologists and local historians expressed concern that natural gas extraction operator Range Resources planned to construct a drilling pad access road through the historic site.

The fort served to protect settlers in the Dutch Fork area from Indian attacks. On March 31, 1782, the fort was attacked, and Ann Hupp led a heroic defense. On Wednesday, May 28, 1947, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker on U.S. 40, 3.5 miles (5.6 km) west of Claysville, noting the importance of Miller's Blockhouse to the history of Pennsylvania. The actual site of the blockhouse is 3 miles (4.8 km) north.

In September 1782, the occupants successfully held off a siege by Indians. The attack on Rice's Fort was recorded in historian's Samuel Kercheval 1883 history A History of the Valley of Virginia. In 1973, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker at U.S. 40 at Lake Road, 3.5 miles (5.6 km) west of Claysville, noting the importance of Rice's Fort to the history of Pennsylvania.

Wolff's Fort was a stockaded log house built in about 1780 by Jacob Wolfe. The Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission describes it as "one of the most important forts in the area." On May 28, 1947, the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission erected a historical marker at U.S. 40, 3.3 miles (5.3 km) southwest of Washington, noting the importance of Wolff's Fort to the history of Pennsylvania.

raw:
data backup habits

Most people treat their digital lives with the same care they would a house key, yet the vast majority ignore where those keys live. We accumulate thousands of photos, documents, and projects on local hard drives that are inherently prone to failure due to mechanical wear or electrical surges. The illusion is that our laptops are eternal vaults, but technology is fragile. A single crash can erase years of memories and business records in seconds, leaving only blank screens and growing panic.

The most robust strategy remains the 3-2-1 rule. You should keep three copies of your critical data. Two of these copies should reside on different storage media, such as your internal drive and an external hard drive. The third copy needs to be stored off-site, typically in a secure cloud service. This redundancy ensures that if one platform fails, you still have at least two reliable options to restore your work without losing everything.

Many argue that cloud storage alone is sufficient, eliminating the need for physical backups. While convenient, subscription-based services introduce a new layer of dependency. If you cancel your plan, lose internet access during an emergency, or encounter a pricing hike, you may find yourself locked out of your own archives. Physical drives offer immediate access regardless of connectivity, making them an indispensable part of any comprehensive safety net.

Automating the process is the single best habit you can adopt. Manual backups are often skipped when life gets busy, leading to months of unbacked-up data. Scheduling software to sync files overnight or to the cloud every hour ensures consistency without requiring daily mental effort. Once set up, it runs in the background, providing peace of mind that every new file is safely copied to an alternate location immediately.

Finally, verify your backups periodically. It is a well-documented horror story for IT professionals to discover that a backup job has been silently failing for months. Run a random restore test once or twice a year to confirm that the files are actually there and readable. A backup that cannot be recovered is not a backup at all, but merely false hope waiting for disaster.

Rural Municipality of Grant No. 372

The Rural Municipality of Grant No. 372 (2016 population: 466) is a rural municipality (RM) in the Canadian province of Saskatchewan within Census Division No. 15 and SARM Division No. 5. The RM's office is located in Vonda.

Holy Trinity Ukrainian Greek Orthodox Church - Constructed in 1924, the church was built by Theodore Yanow and continues to be used as a church. Robert and Adele Schmidt's Double Hip Red Barn - Constructed in 1917. Ss. Peter and Paul Ukrainian Catholic Church (Bodnari Church) - Constructed in 1936, eight kilometers east from the Village of Smuts, the church was constructed by immigrants from the Borschiv region of Ukraine. St. John the Baptist Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church - Constructed near Smuts in 1926, the church was constructed by immigrants from the Borshchiv and Morodenka regions of Ukraine.

In the 2021 Census of Population conducted by Statistics Canada, the RM of Grant No. 372 had a population of 525 living in 190 of its 215 total private dwellings, a change of 12.7% from its 2016 population of 466. With a land area of 659.69 km2 (254.71 sq mi), it had a population density of 0.8/km2 (2.1/sq mi) in 2021. In the 2016 Census of Population, the RM of Grant No. 372 recorded a population of 466 living in 168 of its 187 total private dwellings, a 9.6% change from its 2011 population of 425. With a land area of 666.16 km2 (257.21 sq mi), it had a population density of 0.7/km2 (1.8/sq mi) in 2016.

The RM of Grant No. 372 is governed by an elected municipal council and an appointed administrator that meets on the third Tuesday of every month. The reeve of the RM is Travis Hryniuk while its administrator is Brenda Skakun. The RM's office is located in Vonda.

I am pleased to announce that our company will be moving to a new office space on Main Street, effective Monday, November 18. The new premises will provide us with expanded workstations, modern conference rooms, and a dedicated break area, all designed to support our growing team and enhance collaboration. Over the next few weeks we will be coordinating the logistics, and I wanted to share the key information you'll need to prepare for a smooth transition.
The new address will be 2450 West Oak Avenue, Suite 300, Springfield, 62704. Parking will be available in the underground garage on a first-come, first-served basis, and a shuttle service will run between the old location and the new building from 8:00 am to 6:00 pm each weekday until the move is complete. Please update any client-facing materials, email signatures, and delivery instructions to reflect the new address as soon as possible.
All personal items, including desk supplies and computer equipment, will be packed and labeled by the facilities team on the afternoon of Friday, November 16. If you have any items that require special handling-such as fragile equipment, confidential documents, or plants-please notify the facilities coordinator, Jenna Lee, by the end of the day tomorrow. We will provide moving boxes and packing materials on a first-come, first-served basis, so feel free to stop by the supply closet to collect what you need.
Our IT department will conduct a full network migration over the weekend of November 12-13, which means that internet and phone service may be temporarily unavailable on the evening of Friday, November 16. Please save any important work and ensure that all devices are shut down properly before leaving the office that day. A detailed IT checklist will be distributed later this week to help you prepare.
Thank you for your cooperation and flexibility during this exciting change. I am confident that the new space will offer us a better environment to innovate and grow together. If you have any questions or concerns, do not hesitate to reach out to me directly or to the relocation project team at relocation@company.com.
Best regards,
Michael Alvarez
Chief Operations Officer
Acme Solutions, Inc.

Brandon Curtis

Originally from Norman, Oklahoma, Curtis was friends with members of the Flaming Lips, the Chainsaw Kittens and Tripping Daisy. He and his brother Benjamin (1978-2013) moved to Dallas and formed Secret Machines in the early 2000s with drummer Josh Garza. The trio later moved to New York City, where Benjamin eventually left the band to pursue a career in his previous side project, School of Seven Bells. He has also been a live keyboardist for Interpol since 2010 and was named an official full-time member in 2026.

Curtis's atmospheric keyboard style shows signs of influence from 1970s Krautrock bands like Can as well as progressive rock, space rock and art rock bands such as Pink Floyd, Hawkwind, and Roxy Music. Curtis and his brother Ben also formed UFOFU with Joseph Butcher, touring locally and recording several albums between 1993 and 1997. Curtis was in Captain Audio as well, where he first played with Secret Machines' drummer Josh Garza. Curtis performed lead vocals on "Don't Fall Softly", a track by UK synthpop band Filthy Dukes which appears on their 2009 release "Nonsense In the Dark". He also mixed/produced two records by South African rock band BLK JKS. In June 2010, Curtis joined the touring lineup of Interpol, on keyboards and vocals. In 2012, Brandon joined Interpol front man Paul Banks' live band, and he contributed to Banks' 2012 EP entitled "Julian Plenti Lives...". Curtis contributed to the production, recording, and mixing of EmptyMansions debut album "snakes/vultures/sulfate", released in April 2013. EmptyMansions is the side project of Interpol drummer Sam Fogarino. Curtis toured with EmptyMansions in Spring 2013, on bass/vocals. Curtis has produced three albums for the American post-metal band Russian Circles: Geneva (2009), Empros (2011) and Memorial (2013). On October 30, 2013, Curtis's new band Cosmicide released a new song entitled "Talos' Corpse" and announced a few US tour dates. "Talos' Corpse" was written/produced by Brandon Curtis and mixed by Claudius Mittendorfer, who has previously worked with Paul Banks, Johnny Marr, the Kaiser Chiefs, and more. Cosmicide played three live shows in early 2015 (Philadelphia, Providence RI and Teaneck NJ), playing a nine-song setlist, including Talos' Corpse, consisting mostly of songs from material that is recorded and in a finished state but unreleased. In addition to Brandon, the band consisted of drums, a second keyboardist, and a guitarist. In August of 2020, Secret Machines released an album titled "Awake in the Brain Chamber". Curtis performed keyboard and vocals on the album.

Subject: Proposal for Residential Solar Array Installation and Energy Audit
Dear Mr. Henderson,
Thank you for your interest in making the switch to renewable energy sources for your property on Maple Avenue. After reviewing the preliminary site survey and your recent electricity bills, I am pleased to present this detailed proposal for a residential solar photovoltaic system. The goal of this installation is not only to reduce your monthly utility costs but also to significantly lower your household's carbon footprint over the next twenty-five years. Based on your average monthly consumption of approximately four hundred and fifty kilowatt-hours, we have designed a system that will generate enough power to cover the majority of your daily needs, while allowing you to export surplus energy back to the grid during peak production hours in the midday.
The core component of this project is the installation of eighteen high-efficiency monocrystalline solar panels. These specific units are chosen for their superior performance in varying weather conditions and their reliable long-term degradation rates. Each panel features a ten-year workmanship warranty and a twenty-five-year linear power output guarantee, ensuring that you receive at least eighty percent of the original peak power production even after a quarter-century of use. The estimated total capacity of the array will be roughly fifteen kilowatts, which is optimally sized for a standard four-bedroom home like yours. This configuration allows for comfortable cooling during the summer months while still maintaining positive net metering credits throughout the winter.
Structurally, the mounting system will consist of aluminum rails and L-brackets anchored securely into your roof trusses. Our engineering team has confirmed that your current shingled roof is in excellent structural condition and does not require any reinforcement. The panels will be installed at a thirty-degree tilt angle, which is mathematically optimal for maximizing year-round solar gain in our latitude. This orientation ensures that the array captures the maximum amount of direct and diffuse sunlight, even on overcast days when the sun is obscured by clouds. We will also upgrade your inverter to a hybrid smart inverter model that allows for seamless integration with future home battery storage solutions if you choose to add one later.
The project timeline is estimated to be six to eight weeks from the date of contract signing. This period includes the necessary municipal permitting process, which typically takes two to three weeks depending on local inspection schedules. Once the permits are approved, our certified installation crew will complete the physical mounting and electrical wiring within three business days. The final step involves the utility company inspection and the official permit to operate, which is crucial for activating your net metering account. We handle all interaction with the utility provider to ensure there are no delays or bureaucratic hurdles on your end, allowing you to focus on the convenience and savings the system will bring to your daily life.
Financially, the total installed cost before incentives is twelve thousand five hundred dollars. However, thanks to the federal Investment Tax Credit, you are eligible for a thirty percent credit, reducing the upfront cost significantly. Additionally, your local utility offers a modest per-watt rebate that we have already applied to this quote. We offer flexible financing options with zero percent interest for eighteen months if you prefer to pay over time rather than paying in full. I have attached the formal contract and a detailed energy savings projection for your review. Please let me know if you have any questions or if you would like to schedule a brief call to discuss the next steps so we can move forward with your application for the imminent tax benefits.
Sincerely,
Elena Rodriguez
Senior Account Manager
SunCore Energy Solutions

Subject: Exploring Cloud Storage Options for Our Upcoming Projects
Hi Maya,
I've been reviewing the various cloud storage solutions that could support our growing data needs, and I wanted to share a brief overview of the three platforms that seem most aligned with our requirements. First, Amazon S3 offers robust scalability and a pay-as-you-go pricing model that could help us manage costs as we expand. Its integration with AWS's broader ecosystem also means we can easily tie storage to compute resources for any data-intensive workflows we plan.
Second, Google Cloud Storage provides strong performance for high-throughput workloads and benefits from the same global network that powers Google's services. The nearline and coldline tiers are attractive for archival data, offering lower rates while still keeping retrieval times reasonable. Additionally, their IAM policies are straightforward, which should simplify user access management across teams.
Third, Microsoft Azure Blob Storage is worth considering because of its tight integration with the Microsoft 365 suite we already use. The tiered storage options-hot, cool, and archive-allow us to place data where it makes the most sense financially. Azure's data redundancy options, including geo-redundant storage, give us extra peace of mind for disaster recovery scenarios.
From a security standpoint, all three providers support encryption at rest and in transit, but we'll need to evaluate their key management processes to ensure they meet our compliance standards. It might also be useful to run a short pilot with a subset of our data on each platform to measure actual performance and cost under real-world conditions.
Let me know if you'd like to set up a meeting next week to discuss which option best fits our short-term projects and long-term strategy. I can also prepare a more detailed cost-benefit analysis if that would help.
Best regards, 
Jordan Patel 
IT Infrastructure Manager 
j.patel@company.com

The 1752 Group

The Sexual Harassment in Higher Education (SHHE) Conference, the first UK university conference on staff-to-student sexual harassment, was held at Goldsmiths in December 2015. The conference prompted the organisers, who had spent £1752 on the event, to create a national organisation to identify and address the sexual misconduct of staff within UK universities. The 1752 Group was established in 2016. The Guardian newspaper have been strong supporters of the group.

Dr. Anna Bull, a lecturer in sociology at the University of Portsmouth Dr. Emma Chapman, Royal Astronomical Society Research Fellow, Imperial College London Heidi Hasbrouch, associate director of Qualitative Research at Kantar Public Dr. Tiffany Page, lecturer in sociology at the University of Cambridge Dr. Chryssa Sdrolia, Deputy Curriculum Leader for KS5 English Members of the 1752 Group have given several interviews discussing their priorities. Speaking to the LSE, Dr Page emphasised the need to research and action "it's critical to situate this as being about equal access to education, which comes under the Equality Act 2010 and under institutional responsibilities. Universities need to safeguard and protect their students, but also ensure that they have equal access to resources. Staff sexual misconduct can lead to students interrupting or dropping out of their studies, or having to avoid any situation where they have to be in the same space as that staff member, which affects their studies and access in multiple ways". Dr Anna Bull is running a HEFCE funded project examining university policies, involving focus groups who have experienced staff sexual misconduct. In 2020, the 1752 Group and Ann Olivarius's law firm, McAllister Olivarius, released a report, "Sector Guidance to Address Staff Sexual Misconduct in UK Higher Education."

Sexual misconduct by academic staff is under-researched worldwide, and was last researched in the UK in 1998. The 1752 Group are committed to developing research on sexual misconduct in higher education, and implementing UK-wide policy to protect students. Their strategic priorities include:

Implementing a national code of conduct that clarifies professional boundaries Develop a reporting process for sexual misconduct Establish an independent national office for sexual misconduct advocacy and support Ensure all institutions record data and make publicly available reports on all allegations Address the long-term impact of staff sexual misconduct on those who experience it Implement comprehensive sector-wide and institution-level cultural change In 2011, the NUS' Women's Campaign published Hidden Marks, which found "students who had been subjected to a less serious sexual assault were least likely (< 2 %) to report either to the police or to the institution". The 1752 Group partnered with the National Union of Students to launch the first UK survey into staff sexual misconduct in higher education. The report was published in April 2018. It found that a third of universities have no policy on staff-student relationships, and as a result, less than 10% of students who experienced sexual harassment report the behaviour to their institutions.

Modigliani Quartet

The Modigliani Quartet (French: Quatuor Modigliani) is a French string quartet founded in Paris in 2003 by four close friends, following their studies at the Conservatoire de Paris. Founding violinist Philippe Bernhard left the group in 2016 and was replaced by Amaury Coeytaux.

The founding members studied with the Ysaÿe Quartet in Paris, attended classes by Walter Levin and György Kurtág in 2004, and had the opportunity to work with the Artemis Quartet at the Universität der Künste in Berlin in 2005. They first drew attention by winning the Frits Philips String Quartet competition in Eindhoven (2004), the Vittorio Rimbotti competition in Florence (2005) and the Young Concert Artists Auditions in New York (2006). In 2014 the quartet became artistic directors of the Rencontres musicales d'Évian. After a 13-year pause, this festival, created in 1976 by Antoine Riboud and made famous by its former artistic director Mstislav Rostropovich, began a new life through the joint efforts of the Evian Resort and the Modigliani Quartet.

Amaury Coeytaux: violin Loïc Rio: violin Laurent Marfaing: viola François Kieffer: cello Before joining the group, Coeytaux had been concertmaster of the Orchestre Philharmonique de Radio France.

The Modigliani Quartet plays on four Italian instruments: Amaury Coeytaux plays a 1783 violin by Giovanni Battista Guadagnini, Loic Rio plays a 1734 violin by Alessandro Gagliano, Laurent Marfaing plays a 1660 viola by Luigi Mariani, François Kieffer plays a 1706 cello by Matteo Goffriller (former "Warburg").

Schumann-Wolf-Mendelssohn - Nascor, Ysaÿe Records, 2006 (Schumann: quartet op. 41 no. 1; Wolf: "Italian Serenade"; Mendelssohn: quartet op. 44 no. 1) Haydn - Mirare Records, 2008 (quartets op. 76 no. 4 "Sunrise", op. 74 no. 3 "The rider", op. 54 no. 1) Mendelssohn - Mirare Records, 2010 (quartets in a minor op. 13, in f minor op. 80, Capriccio op. 81 no. 3) Brahms - Mirare Records, 2011 (piano quintet op. 34 w/ Jean-Frédéric Neuburger, Zwei Gësange op. 91 w/ Andrea Hill) Intuition - Mirare Records, 2012 (Arriaga: quartet no. 2, Mozart: quartet no. 6 K 159, Schubert: quartet no. 4 D 46) Debussy-Ravel-Saint-Saëns - Mirare Records, 2013 (Debussy: quartet in g minor, Ravel: quartet in f major, Saint-Saëns: quartet no. 1) Haydn - Mirare Records, 2014 (quartets op. 50 no. 1, op. 76 no. 1, op. 77 no. 1) Schumann - Opus 41 set Schubert - Complete String Quartets, Mirare Records, 2022 Grieg - Smetana - Mirare, 2024

Subject: Thoughts on our current smart home integration
Hi Sarah,
I have been spending quite a bit of time this weekend testing the new mesh network coverage in the basement and the attic. The initial setup was smoother than our last attempt, but I still found a few gaps in the signal near the far corner of the kitchen. This is a critical area because that is where we placed the main smart thermostat and the primary voice assistant hub. If the connection drops there, the entire automated lighting sequence stalls, which defeats the purpose of the system. I did manage to add a small satellite node on the pantry shelf, which seems to have stabilized the link significantly. Please let me know if you notice any lag when you are working from the home office later this week.
While we are on the topic of updates, I want to discuss the security implications of adding these devices to our local network. I know we love the convenience of being able to check the front door camera from our phones while we are away, but I have read several recent alerts about vulnerabilities in older firmware versions. Our current smart locks are running on version two point one, which is nearing its end of life for supported patches. I think it might be wise to look into replacing just the deadbolt mechanism with a newer model that has integrated encryption. We do not need a total overhaul of every device in the house, but the entry points are the most critical. It is a small one-time cost that could save us from major headaches down the line.
Another point I wanted to raise is the energy consumption data we have been tracking over the last month. The smart plugs in the living room have shown a consistent pattern of idle power draw that is higher than advertised. It turns out that the wireless transmitter in each plug uses more electricity when in standby mode than the appliance itself when off. We are looking at an extra ten dollars a month just for the plugs that are not actively controlling refrigerators or heaters. We should probably decide if that cost is worth the minor convenience of turning off lamps from our beds. It is a good reminder that smart technology often comes with hidden trade-offs that are not obvious until we look at the utility bill.
I also wanted to mention that I updated the automation rules for the blinds. Previously, they only opened at sunrise, but I changed the logic to trigger based on actual brightness levels rather than time. This means if it is a cloudy morning, the blinds will remain closed to retain heat, and if the sun breaks through, they will open immediately to maximize natural light. The difference in how the house feels in the morning has been surprising. The space feels larger and brighter without having to manually adjust anything. I think this small change is the most valuable part of the system so far because it supports our daily routine without requiring active input.
Let us schedule a brief call next Tuesday to review the security update schedule and the energy report. I can send over the detailed logs from the network dashboard if you want to see the specific packet loss numbers I mentioned earlier. I want to make sure we are on the same page before we purchase any new hardware. The goal is to have a system that works for us, not one that requires us to work for it. I really do appreciate how much easier it has made monitoring the house, provided we keep the maintenance tasks in perspective. Look out for the calendar invite shortly.
Best regards,
David

lab safety rules

Laboratory work can be thrilling, but it also demands a disciplined approach to safety. The first rule that underlies every successful experiment is to treat the lab as a controlled environment, where each piece of equipment and every chemical has a specific protocol. Before stepping into the workspace, a researcher should take a moment to review the safety data sheets for the substances in use, noting any hazards, required protective gear, and emergency procedures. This habit of preparation reduces the chance of accidental exposure and builds a mindset that respects the power of the materials at hand.

Personal protective equipment, often abbreviated as PPE, is the most visible line of defense. Lab coats, goggles, and gloves should never be considered optional; they are required whenever there is a risk of splashes, fumes, or sharp objects. The coat must be buttoned and the sleeves rolled up to prevent chemicals from pooling on the fabric, while goggles should fit snugly against the face to keep droplets away from the eyes. Gloves must be selected for compatibility with the chemicals being handled, and they should be replaced immediately if they become torn or contaminated. Proper use of PPE can turn a potentially dangerous situation into a manageable one.

The layout of the laboratory itself reinforces safety practices. Walkways must remain clear, and all exits should be unobstructed so that a quick evacuation is possible if an incident occurs. Chemical storage cabinets need to be organized by compatibility, keeping oxidizers away from flammables and acids separate from bases. Spill kits, fire extinguishers, and eyewash stations should be positioned within easy reach, and everyone should know the exact location of each. Regular inspections of these safety devices ensure they are functional when they are most needed.

When it comes to handling chemicals, the principle of "no pipetting by mouth" remains non-negotiable. Use mechanical pipettes or syringes, and never bypass safety equipment to speed up a process. Labeling is another cornerstone: every container must carry a clear, legible label that includes the substance name, concentration, hazard symbols, and date opened. This practice prevents mix-ups and alerts anyone entering the lab to potential dangers, even if they are not the primary user of the material.

Waste disposal is often overlooked, yet it is a critical component of lab safety. Separate bins for hazardous, non-hazardous, and recyclable waste must be maintained, and each should be clearly marked. Contaminated materials should never be placed in regular trash, and solvents or acids should be collected in appropriate containers for neutralization or professional disposal. Following proper waste protocols protects both the laboratory personnel and the broader environment from harmful exposure.

Finally, communication and training are the glue that holds all these rules together. New students and staff should undergo a thorough safety orientation before gaining independent access to the lab, and refresher courses should be offered regularly. Incident reports, even those involving minor spills or near-misses, should be documented and reviewed to identify patterns that may require changes in procedure. By fostering an open culture where safety concerns can be raised without hesitation, a laboratory becomes not only a place of discovery but also a model of responsible scientific practice.

The National Museum of Cultural Heritage is proud to announce its latest major exhibition, "Echoes of the Silk Road: A Journey Through Ancient Crossroads," opening its doors to the public next month. This ambitious presentation invites visitors to explore the rich tapestry of cultures, innovations, and exchanges that defined one of history's most vital networks.

The exhibition meticulously traces the sprawling trade routes that connected East and West for millennia, showcasing how more than just goods traversed continents. Ideas, technologies, artistic styles, and spiritual beliefs flowed freely, shaping diverse societies from imperial China to the Mediterranean. It's a testament to ancient globalization and the profound human capacity for connection.

Visitors will encounter a stunning array of artifacts, many on display for the first time in our region, on loan from prestigious institutions worldwide. Highlights include shimmering Chinese silks that once adorned European nobility, intricate Persian ceramics, Hellenistic gold coinage, and Central Asian frescoes depicting daily life and religious devotion. Maps and navigational instruments from various eras will also illustrate the epic scale of these ancient journeys.

Beyond the artifacts, "Echoes of the Silk Road" offers an immersive experience. Engaging multimedia installations bring ancient landscapes and bustling marketplaces to life, while interactive displays allow visitors to delve deeper into specific trade routes or the unique challenges faced by merchants and travelers. The exhibition aims to foster a deeper understanding of the shared human experience across vast distances and historical divides.

This exhibition is particularly timely, offering perspectives on interconnectedness that resonate powerfully in our contemporary world. It underscores how the threads of commerce and culture, woven thousands of years ago, continue to influence the fabric of modern societies. It's an opportunity to appreciate the enduring legacy of human ingenuity and cooperation.

"Echoes of the Silk Road" will run from October 15th to February 28th. Tickets can be purchased online through the museum's official website or at the admissions desk. Due to anticipated high demand, advanced booking is strongly recommended, especially for weekend visits. Plan your journey into the past and discover the wonders of the Silk Road.

Andrey Igorevich Smolyakov (Russian: Андре́й И́горевич Смоляко́в; born 24 November 1958) is a Soviet and Russian actor and director. He is known for Vysotskiy. Spasibo, chto zhivoy (2011), Stalingrad, and Forbidden Empire.

Smolyakov was born in Podolsk, Moscow Oblast, Russian SFSR, Soviet Union as Andrey Igorevich Smolyakov. For three years he studied at Boris Shchukin Theatre Institute, but switched. In 1980 he graduated from the State Institute of Theatre Arts in a workshop under supervision of Oleg Tabakov. After graduation, he started working as actor on the stage of the Moscow Art Theatre. In 1984-1986 he was associated with the theater "Satirikon". In 1987 he joined the Moscow Studio Theatre Oleg Tabakov. In 2004 he remarried to fashion designer Daria Razumikhina.

Smolyakov made his debut in the film Kiss Dawns (1977). He played the title role in the playwright "Farewell, Mowgli!" based on The Jungle Book by Rudyard Kipling. In 2000 he received the prize of the newspaper Moskovskij Komsomolets in the category "Best Actor" for his role as actor in the play The Lower Depths by Maxim Gorky. In 2002 Andrey Smolyakov, received an award from the Stanislavsky International Fund as well as an award from the Moscow Expert Jury for his role as Brucson in Der Theatermacher, a playwright by Thomas Bernhard. At the awards ceremony at Mosfilm Andrey Smolyakov was the winner of the Golden Eagle Award (Russia) for the best supporting actor in Vysotsky. Thank You For Being Alive as Viktor Bekhteev, a KGB Colonel in Uzbekistan, a drama film about Vladimir Vysotsky. The Russian series Grigorii R, directed by Andrey Malyukov, began on Russian TV Monday 27 October 2014; with Vladimir Mashkov as Grigori Rasputin and Smolyakov as the investigator Smitten.

raw:
The Angel's Game

The Angel's Game (El juego del ángel, 2008) is a prequel to 2001's The Shadow of the Wind, by Spanish author Carlos Ruiz Zafón. The novel marks a return to The Cemetery of Forgotten Books in Barcelona's Raval district, and the Sempere & Sons bookshop. Like The Shadow of the Wind, it was translated into English by Lucia Graves and published in 2009. In Spain it was published in 2008. The planned initial print run broke all publishing records in the country, with one million copies.

The Angel's Game is set in Barcelona in the 1920s and 1930s and follows a young writer, David Martin. In a once-abandoned mansion at the heart of Barcelona, Martín makes his living by writing sensationalist crime stories under a pseudonym. The survivor of a troubled childhood, he has taken refuge in the world of books and spends his nights spinning baroque, "grand guignol" tales about the city's underworld. His own life begins to take on a dramatic bent, in the form of a number of complex relationships: with Pedro Vidal, his patron, with Cristina, the daughter of Vidal's chauffeur, and with Isabella, a young admirer of David and his work. Furthermore, the history of the house he lives in begins to seep into his life - in a locked room within the house lie photographs and letters hinting at the mysterious death of the previous owner. At the same time, he receives a letter from a reclusive but wealthy French editor, Andreas Corelli, who makes him an irresistible offer. He is to write a book unlike anything that has ever existed-an attempt at a new religious work with the power to change hearts and minds. Yet as David begins the work, he realizes that there is a connection between his haunting book and the shadows that surround his home.

The Canadian Press's Maclean's Magazine placed The Angel's Game as number one for their top ten hardcover fiction books for the week ending July 7, 2009. Marley Walker called it "Zafon's ambitious new historic melodrama." USA Today praised The Angel's Game as "a multi-layered confection that combines undying love, magical realism, meditations on religion, the importance of books, and a love affair with the vibrant city of Barcelona." Andrew Reimer said, "Here is more of the same from the author of The Shadow of the Wind " which "is bound to make his fans whoop with joy." However, he also added, "The climax of this new tale is a bit of a mess, with too many twists and turns and perhaps a few too many corpses." Terrence Rafferty wrote that "Ruiz Zafón's flamboyant pulp epic is something altogether sillier, a pact-with-the-devil tale whose only purpose is to give its readers some small intimation of the darker pleasures of the literary arts, the weird thrill of storytelling without conscience." Aravind Adiga of The Age complained that there was "plenty that is ludicrous, clichéd and schematic," but explained that "[l]overs of Barcelona will enjoy Ruiz Zafón's skillful use of that city's architecture--Gothic and Modern."

Bezdrevský potok

The Bezdrevský potok is a stream in the Czech Republic, a left tributary of the Vltava River. It flows through the South Bohemian Region. It is 43.1 km (26.8 mi) long.

The name means 'Bezdrev stream', referring to the Bezdrev fishpond. The name of the pond has its origin in the Czech words bez dřeva, meaning 'without woods'. It referred to a treeless plain on which the pond was established.

The Bezdrevský potok originates in the territory of Brloh in the Bohemian Forest Foothills at an elevation of 681 m (2,234 ft) and flows to Hluboká nad Vltavou, where it enters the Vltava River at an elevation of 371 m (1,217 ft). It is 43.1 km (26.8 mi) long. Its drainage basin has an area of 279.2 km2 (107.8 sq mi). The longest tributaries of the Bezdrevský potok are:

There are 456 bodies of water in the basin area. The basin area is rich in fishponds, especially the area of the lower course of the stream in the České Budějovice Basin. The largest of the fishponds and the third largest pond in the Czech Republic overall is Bezdrev with an area of 365 ha (900 acres), built directly on the Bezdrevský potok. Bezdrev was founded by Vilém II of Pernštejn before 1490. The Bezdrevský potok also supplies several other ponds.

In Netolice, near the dam of the Mnich pond, where the Bezdrevský potok leaves the pond, there are a pair of stone arched bridges, protected as a cultural monument. The older of the bridges probably dates from around 1746, which is the date of the statue that decorates it. The younger bridge was most likely built in the 19th century. The dam of the Bezdrev pond and a bridge over the Bezdrevský potok next to the dam are together protected as a cultural monument. The stone three-arch bridge dates from 1879.

software update notes

Keeping track of software changes is one of the most overlooked yet critical aspects of maintaining a robust digital ecosystem. Whether you are a developer managing a complex microservice architecture or an IT administrator overseeing a network of corporate laptops, update notes serve as the bridge between raw code changes and operational stability. These documents are not merely administrative formalities; they are essential tools for risk assessment and dependency management. In a landscape where applications are interconnected, a single minor patch in a backend library can trigger cascading effects across an entire platform. Understanding exactly what was modified, fixed, or removed allows teams to anticipate conflicts, plan downtime, and ensure that integration tests are properly scoped for the new release.

The structure of effective update notes has evolved significantly over the last decade. While older traditions favored verbose descriptions of every internal refactoring, modern best practices emphasize clarity and relevance. Users and developers alike prefer concise entries that highlight new features, critical bug fixes, and breaking changes. A well-formatted changelog typically categorizes these items distinctly, allowing readers to quickly identify information that impacts their immediate workflow. For instance, a security patch requires a different level of urgency and attention than a cosmetic UI tweak. By prioritizing high-impact changes, documentation becomes a navigable resource rather than an overwhelming wall of text that nobody reads.

However, the challenge lies in maintaining accuracy and consistency across product cycles. Teams often struggle to keep update notes synchronized with the actual codebase, leading to discrepancies between documented behavior and real-world performance. This misalignment can erode trust among users and increase support ticket volume. To mitigate this, many organizations have begun integrating automated generation tools directly into their continuous integration pipelines. These systems can parse commit messages or pull request descriptions to draft initial notes, which are then reviewed and polished by human engineers. This notice serves to inform all residents of the proper process for submitting apartment maintenance requests and to clarify the expectations for both tenants and the property management team. Prompt and accurate reporting of maintenance issues helps keep the building safe, functional, and pleasant for everyone. Please read the following guidelines carefully and keep a copy for future reference.

When a problem arises, tenants should report it through the online portal provided on the resident website, using the "Maintenance Request" form. The form requires a brief description of the issue, the apartment number, and preferred contact details. For matters that cannot be entered online, residents may call the dedicated maintenance line during business hours, or leave a detailed voicemail after the tone. All requests must include the date and time the problem was first observed, as this assists the crew in prioritizing work.

The property management team aims to acknowledge receipt of every request within one hour of submission during regular business hours, and within two hours after hours. Non-emergency issues will be scheduled for a service visit within three business days, while urgent problems such as water leaks, loss of heat, or electrical hazards will be addressed within 24 hours. Tenants will receive a confirmation email with an estimated arrival window and the name of the assigned technician.

Residents are responsible for providing reasonable access to the unit at the scheduled time, securing pets, and removing personal belongings that could obstruct repairs. Maintenance personnel will take care to protect the property and will leave the unit clean after completing the work. If a resident is unavailable at the appointed time, the team will attempt a second visit within the same day; otherwise, the request may be rescheduled at the earliest convenience.

For emergency situations that pose an immediate safety risk, such as gas leaks, exposed wiring, or severe flooding, please call the emergency maintenance line at any hour. For all other inquiries, contact the leasing office at the main phone number or email the maintenance department directly. Your cooperation is essential to maintaining a high standard of living for the entire community.

Stephen Q. Luckett

Stephen Quinton Luckett (October 13, 1938 - August 29, 2025) was an American painter, illustrator, actor, and businessperson from the U.S. state of West Virginia. Originally from Mount Vernon, New York, Luckett was raised in Halltown, West Virginia, where he operated local businesses, taught art, and exhibited his paintings regionally and nationally, including at the Smithsonian Institution. Luckett also acted in film and theatre, directed a local food bank, and illustrated a publication documenting African American heritage in Jefferson County, West Virginia.

Nicknamed "Lucky," Stephen Quinton Luckett was born in Mount Vernon, New York, on October 13, 1938, to Alberta Shelton Luckett Tolbert. In 1948, at the age of ten, he relocated to Halltown, West Virginia, where his grandparents, Benjamin Franklin Shelton, Sr., and Ida Rebecca Edwards Shelton, raised him. Accustomed to the illuminated nighttime environment of an urban setting, Luckett initially found West Virginia's nighttime strikingly dark upon his arrival by train. However, he subsequently expressed his appreciation for the natural beauty of the state, noting that his preferred colors of "brown-yellow-gold and greens" reflected his love for West Virginia and the state's influence on him.

In his early life, Luckett established a grocery store and sign painting business known as Lucky's Bait and Sign Shop in Halltown, in addition to operating a bookkeeping service. He pursued painting independently, successfully completing a fine arts correspondence course through the Famous Artists School in 1967. Luckett painted both signs and fine art pieces, including landscapes and portraits. In addition, he instructed art classes. Luckett's earlier exhibitions occurred in 1965 at the Potomac Vista Casa de Regalos store in Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, followed by the Washington County Museum of Fine Arts in Hagerstown, Maryland, in 1968. Luckett subsequently exhibited his work at the Mountain Heritage Arts and Crafts Show in Jefferson County, West Virginia, the Virginia National Bank in Reston, Virginia, the Harpers Ferry Art Show and Festival in Harpers Ferry, the Jefferson County Fair art shows (where he won several first place awards), the Brunswick-Potomac River Festival in Brunswick, Maryland, and the Shepherd College Art Festival, the Shenandoah Downs in Charles Town, West Virginia, the Blakely Bank and Trust Company, the Peoples Bank, and the Bank of Charles Town. In 1973, Luckett exhibited a collection of drawings and paintings at the Brunswick Public Library in Brunswick, as part of the Brunswick-Potomac Foundation's Year-Round Art Program. In 1981, Luckett's painting The Winner was selected by the National Museum of American Art, Smithsonian Institution, for the exhibition, "More Than Land or Sky: Art from Appalachia," which toured thirteen Appalachian states in the early 1980s. Luckett noted the Smithsonian's selection of his painting for this exhibition as a career high point. In 1982, six of his works, including Country Scenes and The Old Barn, were exhibited at the Oglebay Institute in Wheeling, West Virginia. His work also featured in the 2018 "Four African-American Artists from Jefferson County" exhibition at the Jefferson County Museum in Charles Town. In addition, he illustrated the 1994 publication, Historical Digest of Jefferson County, West Virginia's African American Congregations, 1864-1994.

Luckett appeared in the films Ghost Stories of Harpers Ferry (1974), portraying one of John Brown's men, and Pudd'nhead Wilson (1984). In 1977, he portrayed Shields Green in the play The Anvil about John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry at the Jefferson County Courthouse in Charles Town. Luckett also appeared in the play The Little Foxes at the Old Opera House in Charles Town in 1982.

Luckett remained a lifelong resident of Halltown, West Virginia, operating his business and, during midlife, serving as a notary and tax preparer. In the early 1990s, he joined the Beware Against Drugs, Inc. free food program, and became its director in 1995, personally funding the program during times of financial shortfall. Also in 1995, Luckett was interviewed regarding the history of the Halltown Union Colored Sunday School for the book Black Heritage Sites: An African American Odyssey and Finder's Guide. By 2018, Luckett had retired from other vocations but continued preparing income taxes. While he held many professions, Luckett identified painting as his first love, equating the completion of a painting with profound personal satisfaction. He died on August 29, 2025, with a memorial service held on September 18, 2025, at Eckles-Spencer and Norton Funeral Home in Halltown.

Stephen Quinton Luckett (October 13, 1938 - August 29, 2025) was an American painter, illustrator, actor, and businessperson from the U.S. state of West Virginia. Originally from Mount Vernon, New York, Luckett was raised in Halltown, West Virginia, where he operated local businesses, taught art, and exhibited his paintings regionally and nationally, including at the Smithsonian Institution. Luckett also acted in film and theatre, directed a local food bank, and illustrated a publication documenting African American heritage in Jefferson County, West Virginia.

Nicknamed "Lucky," Stephen Quinton Luckett was born in Mount Vernon, New York, on October 13, 1938, to Alberta Shelton Luckett Tolbert. In 1948, at the age of ten, he relocated to Halltown, West Virginia, where his grandparents, Benjamin Franklin Shelton, Sr., and Ida Rebecca Edwards Shelton, raised him. Accustomed to the illuminated nighttime environment of an urban setting, Luckett initially found West Virginia's nighttime strikingly dark upon his arrival by train. However, he subsequently expressed his appreciation for the natural beauty of the state, noting that his preferred colors of "brown-yellow-gold and greens" reflected his love for West Virginia and the state's influence on him.

In his early life, Luckett established a grocery store and sign painting business known as Lucky's Bait and Sign Shop in Halltown, in addition to operating a bookkeeping service. He pursued painting independently, successfully completing a fine arts correspondence course through the Famous Artists School in 1967. Luckett painted both signs and fine art pieces, including landscapes and portraits. In addition, he instructed art classes. Luckett's earlier exhibitions occurred in 1965 at the Potomac Vista Casa de Regalos store in Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, followed by the Washington County Museum of Fine Arts in Hagerstown, Maryland, in 1968. Luckett subsequently exhibited his work at the Mountain Heritage Arts and Crafts Show in Jefferson County, West Virginia, the Virginia National Bank in Reston, Virginia, the Harpers Ferry Art Show and Festival in Harpers Ferry, the Jefferson County Fair art shows (where he won several first place awards), the Brunswick-Potomac River Festival in Brunswick, Maryland, and the Shepherd College Art Festival, the Shenandoah Downs in Charles Town, West Virginia, the Blakely Bank and Trust Company, the Peoples Bank, and the Bank of Charles Town. In 1973, Luckett exhibited a collection of drawings and paintings at the Brunswick Public Library in Brunswick, as part of the Brunswick-Potomac Foundation's Year-Round Art Program. In 1981, Luckett's painting The Winner was selected by the National Museum of American Art, Smithsonian Institution, for the exhibition, "More Than Land or Sky: Art from Appalachia," which toured thirteen Appalachian states in the early 1980s. Luckett noted the Smithsonian's selection of his painting for this exhibition as a career high point. In 1982, six of his works, including Country Scenes and The Old Barn, were exhibited at the Oglebay Institute in Wheeling, West Virginia. His work also featured in the 2018 "Four African-American Artists from Jefferson County" exhibition at the Jefferson County Museum in Charles Town. In addition, he illustrated the 1994 publication, Historical Digest of Jefferson County, West Virginia's African American Congregations, 1864-1994.

Luckett appeared in the films Ghost Stories of Harpers Ferry (1974), portraying one of John Brown's men, and Pudd'nhead Wilson (1984). In 1977, he portrayed Shields Green in the play The Anvil about John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry at the Jefferson County Courthouse in Charles Town. Luckett also appeared in the play The Little Foxes at the Old Opera House in Charles Town in 1982.

Luckett remained a lifelong resident of Halltown, West Virginia, operating his business and, during midlife, serving as a notary and tax preparer. In the early 1990s, he joined the Beware Against Drugs, Inc. free food program, and became its director in 1995, personally funding the program during times of financial shortfall. Also in 1995, Luckett was interviewed regarding the history of the Halltown Union Colored Sunday School for the book Black Heritage Sites: An African American Odyssey and Finder's Guide. By 2018, Luckett had retired from other vocations but continued preparing income taxes. While he held many professions, Luckett identified painting as his first love, equating the completion of a painting with profound personal satisfaction. He died on August 29, 2025, with a memorial service held on September 18, 2025, at Eckles-Spencer and Norton Funeral Home in Halltown.

Residents of the Oakhaven district have noted a steady increase in activity levels over the past quarter, which warrants a collective review of our community safety protocols. While no major incidents have been recorded recently, the presence of unfamiliar vehicles and occasional loitering near the main park entrances has sparked concern among long-time inhabitants. This document serves to outline current best practices and remind everyone of their role in maintaining a secure environment for all members of our neighborhood, from families with young children to elderly residents who may be more vulnerable to environmental risks.

First and foremost, visibility remains the most effective deterrent against potential misconduct. Residents are encouraged to ensure that exterior lighting is functional and properly angled to illuminate doorways, walkways, and vehicle entry points. Dark corners and unlit gardens can inadvertently create hiding spots that compromise security. Simple measures, such as motion-sensor lights or replacing burnt-out bulbs promptly, significantly reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access. Furthermore, keeping hedges trimmed at a height of no more than three feet along property lines helps prevent visual obstructions that might hide criminal activity while allowing neighbors to monitor one another's perimeters naturally.

Digital communication channels must be utilized responsibly and efficiently to prevent alarm fatigue. The community app should be reserved for verified security concerns, immediate hazards, or urgent assistance requests rather than social updates or minor complaints. When reporting a suspicious incident, provide specific details such as time, location, direction of travel, and physical descriptions of individuals or vehicles involved. Vague reports dilute the urgency of legitimate threats and can lead to delayed responses from law enforcement. We ask each household to designate a primary contact person for emergency coordination to streamline information flow during critical moments.

Home fortification requires a balance between security and aesthetics. Deadbolts should be installed on all exterior doors, and windows on ground floors should be fitted with high-quality lock sliders or security bars. It is also advisable to avoid displaying valuable items in plain view from the street, as this can signal to potential intruders that a home is a target. Regular maintenance of gates and fences, ensuring they latch securely and remain free of damage, adds another layer of physical defense. While these steps do not guarantee absolute safety, they significantly increase the effort required for any unlawful entry, thereby discouraging opportunistic crimes.

Finally, fostering a sense of cohesive community watch is paramount. Getting to know your neighbors, even on a basic level, creates a network of eyes that can spot anomalies faster than any camera system. A friendly wave or a brief conversation can establish trust and ensure that if a neighbor notices something out of the ordinary, they are comfortable reaching out for verification or assistance. We encourage participation in the upcoming quarterly safety meeting, scheduled for the first Saturday of next month, where we will review recent police statistics and discuss further enhancements to our collective vigilance. Together, our proactive approach and mutual support form the strongest shield for the Oakhaven neighborhood.

The annual review cycle for our tabletop gaming library is now open to all staff members and registered patrons. This process is essential for maintaining the quality and relevance of our collection, ensuring that every game on the shelf meets the high standards of playability, condition, and educational value expected by our community. By engaging in this rigorous assessment, we collectively curate an experience that remains fresh, diverse, and accessible for players of all skill levels, from novice families to competitive veterans.

Reviewers should begin by inspecting the physical integrity of each component. Check for missing pieces, warped boards, faded card faces, and damaged tokens. The state of the instruction manual is particularly critical, as confusing or illegible directions significantly detract from the user experience. If a game is missing more than three minor components or has major structural damage that cannot be repaired, it should be flagged for immediate repair or retirement. Consistency in these checks ensures that when a patron picks up a copy, they can begin playing within minutes without troubleshooting mechanical deficits.

Beyond physical condition, evaluate the gameplay mechanics and thematic coherence. Play through a full session to identify any rules ambiguities, design flaws, or engagement drops. Note whether the theme complements or hinders the mechanics. For instance, a heavy strategy game with a light humorous theme might feel disjointed, potentially confusing new players. Document specific moments where the group hesitated or where the win conditions felt unbalanced. These qualitative observations provide invaluable context that simple star ratings cannot capture, helping future users set accurate expectations before they commit to a play session.

The review form requires a concise summary of strengths and weaknesses, along with a recommended age range and group size. Avoid subjective language that excludes potential players; instead, focus on objective descriptors such as competitive intensity, component complexity, and setup duration. Include specific notes on any necessary house rules that improved the experience, as these can often be generalized to benefit the broader community. This data will be aggregated to inform our purchasing decisions, allowing us to discontinue underperforming titles and invest in new releases that align with demonstrated patron preferences and community feedback.

Submissions are due by the end of the month and can be uploaded to the internal staff portal under the library maintenance section. Please ensure your text is professional and constructive, aiming to improve the collection rather than criticize individual designers or publishers. Your detailed insights directly shape the tangible value of our shared space, fostering an environment where every game night is successful. Thank you for your continued dedication to preserving the longevity and joy of board gaming through diligent stewardship and thoughtful curation efforts.

Expressway S17 (Poland)

Expressway S17 or express road S17 (pl. Droga ekspresowa S17) is a Polish highway which, when completed, will run from Warsaw through Lublin to the border crossing with Ukraine at Hrebenne/Rava-Ruska. As of May 2026, 163 km (101 mi) out of planned 310 km (190 mi) are opened to traffic: the main section running from Warsaw through Lublin to Piaski, as well as bypasses of Tomaszów Lubelski and Hrebenne. The section from Piaski to the border with Ukraine is planned to get opened in stages from 2027 to 2031.

In December 2009, the bidding process was started for the contracts to build the 66 km (41 mi) section around Lublin, from Kurów to Piaski. It forms the common route of expressways S12 and S17 and includes the east-west bypass of Lublin. The construction of this section started in 2010, with the first 13 km section to be opened to traffic in late 2012 and the rest in 2014. The section between Warsaw and Lublin was to be finished by 2015, but with subsequent reductions in government spending on infrastructure, the investment was delayed. The section was constructed in the design-build system starting late 2015 and early 2016, and the road was opened to traffic in 2019 and 2020. The road southeast of Lublin has smaller traffic density and received a lower priority, except for the bypass of Tomaszów Lubelski which was opened in 2021 (first carriageway) and 2023 (second carriageway). In January 2024 contractors were selected to build two sections of the segment between Piaski and Zamość (16,6 km Piaski - Łopiennik; 18,8 km Krasnystaw - Izbica ) with completion planned for 2027. Three sections between Zamość and Hrebenne are currently under construction (Zamość Wschód - Zamość Południe, Zamość Południe - Tomaszów Lubelski, Tomaszów Lubelski - Hrebenne), with completion planned for 2027. Opening of the expressway between Piaski and Ukraine's border is expected from 2027 until 2031 depending on the section.

In Warsaw, the S17 expressway will serve as the eastern bypass of the city. Apart from the southernmost section from Lubelska to Zakręt, which was opened in 2022, the construction timetable is not yet set due to the environmental permit having been challenged in the courts.

Marcus Lloyd

Lloyd, the eldest of four children of opera singer Robert Lloyd, grew up in Finchley, London. Having attended a local comprehensive school, he went on to study physics at Worcester College, Oxford and then drama writing with playwright Bernard Kops while supporting himself working in the cloakroom of the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden.

In 1995 his first play, Taking Pictures was directed by Gerard Murphy. It starred Kevin Elyot and Rebecca Thorn and was a winner in the New London Radio Playwrights Festival. The following year he won BBC Television's Double Exposure screenwriting award for his 60-minute television play, A Relative Stranger, which was first broadcast on BBC2 in 1996 starring Siobhan Redmond (Alison Fraiman), Suzanna Hamilton (Jenny Bell), Ioan Gruffudd (Nigel Fraiman) and Jason Isaacs (Peter Fraiman). Dead Certain, his first stage play, was first produced in 1999 at the Theatre Royal, Windsor and starred Jenny Seagrove (Elizabeth) and Steven Pinder (Michael). It has since received numerous other productions in the UK, New Zealand, Australia, Singapore and the US, including a year-long run in San Francisco. In 2001 his screenplay Cuckoo won the prestigious Oscar Moore Foundation Screenwriting Prize and the award, presented by patron Emma Thompson, enabled him to devote himself full-time to writing. Other screenplays include, Wake Up Dead for Stephen Garrett and Paul Webster at Kudos Film & Television, and a screen adaptation of Brian Aldiss's classic science fiction story, Non-Stop for Lightship Films. In 2015 "Dead Certain" was adapted for Polish TV and broadcast on TVP1 under the title Zabojcza Pewnosc on 23 March (Dir. Mariusz. With: Magdalena Cielecka and Grzegorz Malecki) Other work includes the short films: To The Grave; Miriam (which featured Roger Lloyd-Pack in his final screen appearance); and The Interview (2007); the radio plays Vacant Possession and The True Story of Mr. Box; and the children's stage play "The Front To Back Toyshop."

The Office of Student Financial Aid announces that the application portal for the Meridian Foundation Endowed Scholarship is now open. Eligible graduating seniors who have maintained a minimum cumulative grade point average of 3.5 are encouraged to submit their applications by the strict deadline of May 15th at midnight Eastern Time. This scholarship aims to support students who have demonstrated not only academic excellence but also a commitment to community service and professional leadership. Applicants should carefully review the specific criteria outlined in the attached description, as the selection committee places significant weight on the alignment between the candidate's goals and the foundation's mission of fostering ethical business practices. Late submissions will not be considered under any circumstances, and technical issues should not be used as an excuse for missed deadlines.

Required materials include a complete and certified official transcript from all previously attended institutions, sent directly from the registrar's office by the March 1st application portal close date. Applicants must also provide two distinct letters of recommendation, one from an academic faculty member who can speak to their intellectual capabilities and another from a professional supervisor or community leader who can attest to their character and work ethic. These letters must be uploaded through the online platform in PDF format. If any requirement is missing, the application will be deemed incomplete and will be automatically disqualified from the review process. We strongly advise students to request their transcripts and letters of recommendation at least two weeks before the deadline to allow for normal bureaucratic processing times.

The personal statement is a critical component of this application, and candidates should dedicate sufficient time to drafting a reflective and coherent narrative. Mahmoud al-Werfalli

Mahmoud Mustafa Busayf al-Werfalli (Arabic: محمود مصطفى بوسيف الورفلي; 1978 - 24 March 2021) was a Libyan general, commander in al-Saiqa, an elite unit of the Libyan National Army, one of the warring factions in Libya's civil war since 2014. Al-Werfalli was indicted in 2017 in the International Criminal Court for the war crimes of murder and ordering the murder of non-combatants under article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Rome Statute. As of 6 April 2019, the ICC had two outstanding warrants for al-Werfalli's arrest. He was assassinated on 24 March 2021 in Benghazi.

Al-Werfalli was born in 1978. He was a member of the Warfalla tribe, which was loyal to former Libyan ruler Muammar Gaddafi and from which many members of Gaddafi's security forces were recruited.

Al-Werfalli began his career in the Libyan Army in 2000 after graduating from the country's military college. He eventually became a member of the elite al-Saiqa unit and remained a member when the Libyan Civil War against Gaddafi's rule began in 2011. Soon thereafter al-Saiqa, under the command of Wanis Bukhmada, defected and joined the rebels. Following the end of Gaddafi's rule, al-Saiqa aligned itself with the Libyan National Army, led by Khalifa Haftar, and fought against the Shura Council of Benghazi Revolutionaries in and around the city of Benghazi from 2014 to 2017 in a battle for control of the city. By at least 2017, al-Werfalli was a regional commander of al-Saiqa and oversaw at least one detention center. In that year al-Werfalli gained international notoriety by appearing in videos posted by al-Saiqa's social media accounts that depicted him executing or ordering the execution of prisoners. In total 7 videos were published. One video in particular allegedly depicted the execution of 20 men. Al-Werfalli's actions were singled out by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, which documented several of these incidents and called for a full investigation.

Mahmoud al-Werfalli was indicted on 15 August 2017 with the war crime of murder with regard to the situation in Libya. The arrest warrant against him alleges that he "appears to be directly responsible for the killing of, in total, 33 persons in Benghazi or surrounding areas, between on or before 3 June 2016 and on or around 17 July 2017, either by personally killing them or by ordering their execution." The arrest warrant notes that in seven incidents, which were videoed and posted on al-Saiqa's social media accounts, al-Werfalli either appeared to order the execution, or conducted the execution himself, of prisoners. The Court notes in the arrest warrant that "the executions were exceptionally cruel, dehumanising and degrading." Two days after the Court issued the warrant of arrest, the Libyan National Army (LNA) announced that it had arrested al-Werfalli and that he was under investigation. On 24 January 2018, he was accused of executing 10 prisoners in Benghazi. Automatically after that, an Interpol red notice against him, on behalf of International Criminal Court, was issued.

In December 2019, the US Treasury Department included Al-Werfalli on its sanctions list, accusing him of committing serious human rights violations. In its statement, the US Treasury said that Al-Werfalli was filmed on January 24, 2018, "carrying out a mass execution of ten unarmed detainees in Benghazi. After each detainee was shot in the head one by one, Al-Werfalli fired freely on a group of ten detainees who were executed." In September 2020, he was also sanctioned by the EU, for the same criminal charges.

On 24 March 2021, Libyan media quoted a spokesman for the "Libyan National Army" as confirming that "the military commander, Mahmoud Al-Werfalli, was killed in Benghazi." Al-Werfalli died after his car was hit by bullets near Al-Arab Medical University in Benghazi. His brother was injured in the attack and was taken to intensive care.
